Stronger killer cells could also help patients whose own immune systems are weakened by transplant drugs.
plos-pone-0005697:
Alana Conti and colleagues studied in 2009 how alcohol changes a key learning site in the mouse brain. Mice lacking two enzymes, AC1 and AC8, react to alcohol in unusual ways. Those enzymes help nerve cells adjust the strength of their links, a base of memory.

The team found that the two enzymes start a self-correcting response at the synapse when alcohol arrives. This presynaptic response acts like a brake, steadying the circuit. Knowing which molecules set that brake helps explain why alcohol's effects differ between people. It also marks paths for drugs aimed at problem drinking.
plos-pone-0005797:
Iain Anderson and co-authors read the genomes of a little-studied order of methane-making microbes in 2009. Methanomicrobiales make methane in swamps, guts, and sediments. By ribosomal genes they sit near one class of methanogens, yet their metabolism looks like another's.

Full genomes let the team sort them into three classes with distinct toolkits. That order sharpens how scientists model methane output from nature, a greenhouse concern. It also shows how genome reads can settle mismatches between a family tree and a lifestyle. These microbes punch far above their size in climate terms.
plos-pone-0006397:
A virus that helps a parasitic wasp turns out to sit where three virus families meet. Yves Bigot and colleagues studied the symbiotic ascovirus DpAV4a in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. The virus markedly increases its wasp vector's fitness by raising survival of wasp eggs and larvae inside moth hosts.

The authors place the virus at the evolutionary intersection of iridoviruses, ascoviruses, and ichnoviruses. Shared ancestry among large DNA viruses is written in its genome. A wasp's partner virus thus informs the whole family tree. Symbiosis and evolution meet in one genome.
plos-pone-0006497:
Myriam Ermonval and co-authors studied two membrane proteins that meet in PLOS ONE in 2009. The cellular prion protein is attached to cell membranes and is abundant in lipid rafts, ordered patches of membrane. This protein is absolutely required for the neurodegeneration seen in prion diseases. The team examined its interaction with tissue non-specific alkaline phosphatase in membrane microdomains.

Partners of the prion protein may explain what it does in healthy cells. They may also show how it turns harmful. Membrane microdomains are where many signals are organized. Finding a partner there adds a piece to the prion puzzle, which still lacks a full picture of normal function.
plos-pone-0006597:
Saeid Taheri and co-authors correlated two imaging measures after stroke in rats in PLOS ONE in 2009. Variations in apparent diffusion coefficient of water and blood-brain barrier permeability after ischemia have both been suggested as injury markers. The correlation between them was their question. Ischemia is the loss of blood flow that causes stroke damage.

They mapped spatiotemporal correlations: how the two measures relate across space and time. If they track together, one scan may stand in for both. If they diverge, each tells a different part of the injury story. Such mapping helps interpret brain scans after stroke.
plos-pone-0009397:
Xiaojuan Chen and co-authors published this diabetes imaging study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Tissues outside the pancreas, like the liver, might be coaxed into making insulin. That would open a new route to treat diabetes. Watching insulin gene activity in those tissues, inside a living animal, was the challenge.

The team used mice carrying a glowing reporter tied to the insulin gene switch. Bioluminescence imaging let them detect insulin gene expression outside the pancreas in diabetic mice. A live readout like this can follow attempts to grow new insulin sources over time. It turns an invisible gene switch into a measurable signal.
plos-pone-0009497:
Gitit Shahaf, Michael Cancro, and Ramit Mehr used math models of B cell life in PLOS ONE in 2010. B cells make antibodies. Those that react too strongly without proper support signals are removed. This culling happens as B cells mature in the marrow and later in the body. The team modeled how long cells live and where losses occur.

Their model points to a shared death niche for new and mature B cells. In other words, both stages face removal in a like setting. That finding maps the immune system's quality control in a new way. It helps explain how the body prunes risky cells at more than one stage.
plos-pone-0009597:
Michael Moore and colleagues reported a whale rescue method in PLOS ONE in 2010. North Atlantic right whales are among the rarest large whales. Many die tangled in fishing gear. Rescue boats often cannot get close, because the whales evade them. The team tried sedating two free swimming whales at sea. Careful doses were given by injection to calm them.

Once sedated, the whales let boats approach for disentanglement work. The approach raised the chance of removing gear that would otherwise kill them. Sedation at sea carries risks, so dosing had to be exact. The study shows it can be done, giving rescuers a new option for a species near extinction.
plos-pone-0010397:
Katarina Järlestedt and co-workers asked whether calming a brain scar response changes injury size in newborn mice, for PLOS ONE in 2010. After brain injury, star-shaped support cells react and build up two structural proteins. This reaction is called gliosis. In adult mice missing those proteins, the reaction is blunted. The team tested baby mice with oxygen shortage plus reduced blood flow, a model of newborn brain injury.

Even with gliosis weakened, the injured area stayed the same size. So the support-cell reaction may not drive early damage, at least in newborns. That matters because some treatments aim at gliosis itself. If it does not set injury size, efforts should target other steps. Negative results like this save a field wasted effort.
plos-pone-0010497:
Hania Köver and Shaowen Bao proposed that brain flexibility stores our prior expectations in PLOS ONE in 2010. Perception blends fresh sensory input with what past experience predicts. Ambiguous signals get pulled toward the expected reading. How neurons physically keep those priors was unknown. Other theorists had suggested changing response patterns that shift over time. The authors advanced cortical plasticity, lasting change in cortex connections, as the storage mechanism.

If priors live in plastic connections, learning literally rewires perception. That would explain why expectations are stable yet updatable. The idea connects a math theory of perception, Bayesian inference, to brain hardware. It suggests experiments that track connection change as priors form. Theory papers like this steer the next round of experiments.
plos-pone-0010597:
Emmanuel Boucrot and colleagues questioned a textbook claim about how cells take in cargo, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Cells swallow material by building small coated pits on their surface. A helper complex called AP-2 was long thought to be required for every pit.

The team lowered AP-2 levels in cells far below normal. Some cargo still entered cells at a healthy rate. Other cargo did depend on AP-2, as expected. So the helper is vital for certain loads but not for all. The result forces a more careful account of how coated pits form and work.
plos-pone-0010697:
Erich Loza Telleria and colleagues studied gut enzymes in the sand fly that spreads leishmaniasis, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Lutzomyia longipalpis carries Leishmania parasites from person to person. Before a parasite can thrive in the fly, it must survive the fly's gut, where digestive enzymes called trypsins break down the blood meal.

The team measured when and how strongly the fly makes these trypsins. They also tested whether the parasite changes that pattern. Parasites that blunt digestion gain a safer start in the gut. Knowing the timing of the enzyme wave suggests when the parasite is weakest, a useful fact for blocking spread inside the fly.
plos-pone-0010797:
Julia Nowack and colleagues recorded body temperature in a small African primate, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The lesser bushbaby, Galago moholi, lives in dry savanna where food and water swing with the seasons. Torpor, a controlled drop in body temperature, saves energy. Among primates, true torpor was thought to be a lemur specialty.

Bushbabies in the wild dropped into torpor when conditions turned harsh. Their temperature fell for hours, then rose again on better days. Torpor on demand in a non-lemur primate widens the trait's known range in our own order. It also hints that early primates may have had more flexible body control than living species suggest.
plos-pone-0010897:
Maria Martin, Shaguna Seth, Dimitrios Koutsonanos and co-authors published this vaccine study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Flu shots given by muscle injection raise good blood antibodies, but protection might improve if the airways, where flu enters, were defended too. The team explored vaccination through the skin, a needle-free route, paired with natural compounds that rouse the immune system.

In their experiments, inactivated flu virus delivered across the skin, together with retinoic acid or oleic acid, drew immune scout cells toward nearby lymph nodes. The responses were strong, lasted a long time, and protected animals against a lethal flu challenge. Martin and colleagues show that route and additives together can upgrade a standard vaccine. Skin delivery could also ease mass vaccination, since it avoids needles and trained injectors.
plos-pone-0010997:
Viviane Hénaux, Michael Samuel and Christine Bunck published this bird flu modeling study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Predicting how bird flu moves through wild birds is key to protecting farms and people. Yet the most dangerous strains are so rarely found in wild birds that their behavior there is guesswork. The authors used modeling to fuse what laboratory and field studies do know.

They built a standard epidemic model with susceptible, exposed, infectious, and recovered classes, and fed it parameters from published challenge experiments, split by bird age and virus virulence. Infection led to shedding within a day or two, followed by a relatively short infectious period. Hénaux and colleagues also flag where ignorance is greatest. Their synthesis tells surveillance programs which measurements would most improve risk forecasts for wild waterfowl.
plos-pone-0011097:
Bull, Jessop and Whiteley examined Komodo dragons in PLOS ONE in 2010. These giant lizards bite large prey, which often escape at first but die later. A long held idea said germs in dragon saliva infect the wound and help finish the prey.

The authors weighed the evidence for that septic bite idea, looking at both its history and its ecology. Testing a famous claim matters because newer work pointed to venom instead. Their review helps settle what really makes a dragon bite so deadly. It is also a case study in how striking animal stories should be checked.
plos-pone-0011197:
Hsieh reported a land walking fish in PLOS ONE in 2010. One marine fish can move onto land, a rare feat for a fully water based species. The author studied the new movement pattern, involving fins and body, that makes that water to land shift possible.

A single locomotor innovation opened a whole new habitat to this fish. That mirrors, in miniature, the great move of early vertebrates onto land. Watching a living fish manage the shift shows what mechanical problems had to be solved. The case gives evolution research a present day test bed for an ancient transition.
plos-pone-0011297:
Marozeau, Innes-Brown, Grayden and colleagues tested sight and sound together in PLOS ONE in 2010. Listeners must separate one melody from another, a task called stream segregation. The team asked whether visual cues help that separation, and whether musicians and non musicians benefit differently.

Watching did assist the ears in sorting sound streams in their tests. Cross sensory help like this reflects how the brain normally works in a multisensory world. Musicianship shaped the size of the effect, adding a training angle. The findings inform hearing science and may comfort music lovers with hearing loss who lean on sight.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1297:
The British Chiefs of Staff issued this memorandum on 18 July 1945. Like its American mates, it did the staff thinking that leaders later turned into choices. The British run of papers in the volume mirrors the American one, date by date.

London's chiefs wrote with their own burdens in view: a tired army, a vast navy bill, and duties from Europe to Asia. This note carries that view at the talks' start. It is preserved in an American volume because the allied staffs shared their paper. That sharing is itself a fact about how the Western war was run.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1397:
Jefferson Caffery, the American ambassador in France, wrote to Georges Bidault, the French foreign minister, on 1 August 1945. The volume prints six Caffery letters to Bidault from the turn of August 1945. The letters came as the Potsdam Conference reached its close in Germany.

France's absence from Potsdam rankled in Paris, and Bidault worked to win a place in the councils that would run Germany. Caffery's letters carried the American answers, welcome or not. This letter was written on the day the Potsdam Protocol was signed. It shows the settlement's second tier being built in parallel. A shut-out ally was being brought into the peace, on terms set here. The run of letters is the volume's fullest view of that process.
frus-1945-50-intel-d97:
Magruder wrote to McCloy again on 25 October 1945, keeping his near-monthly rhythm of reports to his patron. The text comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States volume that looks back at American intelligence work from 1945 to 1950.

By late October the SSU's position had a shape: tolerated in the War Department, eyed by State, and priced hard by the Budget Bureau. Magruder's letters steered between those forces. Readers should attend to what a chief in his spot could and could not say. He could plead usefulness; he could not command a future. The thread's interest lies in that narrow path, walked in careful prose through the whole autumn of decision.
frus-1945-50-intel-d197: A text titled "Memorandum for the File" bears the date 17 July 1946. It survives in print as document 197 of the State Department's Foreign Relations volume on intelligence, 1945 to 1950. No CIA yet existed: a board called the National Intelligence Authority ran the work, with the Central Intelligence Group as its staff. The form is a note to the file: no request and no order.
frus-1945-50-intel-d297:
The memorandum of 6 August 1948 names the Record by the Chief of the Special Procedures Group (Cassady) as the man it was written for. The Office of the Historian kept it as document 297 in the Foreign Relations intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. Reform of the CIA was in the air, with the Dulles survey under way and each agency guarding its own role.

A record memo speaks to the future reader more than to any chief: it exists so the file tells the truth later. Such notes anchor the rest of the paper trail around them. Alone it is a page; in sequence it is evidence of how a state taught itself a new trade.
frus-1945-50-intel-d397:
Robert Schow, the CIA's assistant director for special operations, wrote to planning chief J. Prichard Childs on 26 August 1949. The memo is document 397 in the Foreign Relations volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

Special operations meant secret work abroad, the most guarded part of the young agency. Schow's office ran that work while Childs tried to fit it into one government wide plan. Their exchange shows the pull between secret action and central control that marked the CIA from its first years. Coordination papers like this one rarely name foes or lands, but they set the frame for all later work.
frus-1861-d97:
A reply dated 14 October 1861 went from William H. Seward to Lord Lyons in Washington. The letter is document 97 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

A same day answer was swift work for the age. Seward and Lyons kept a brisk exchange through that autumn, claim by claim. This reply shows the Secretary meeting British pressure with equal speed, in the hope that quick words would keep small points small. Quick answers also denied London any ground to claim its notes went unheeded. Quick words, in that season, were a form of respect that both sides prized.
frus-1861-d197:
Cassius Clay wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 7 June 1861. The dispatch is document 197 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Clay's first report in the file comes from his new post in Russia. He found a court that spoke warmly of the Union. His June letter began a run of good news from the north that ran through the whole war. His run of reports from Russia forms the happiest thread in the year's record. The happiest thread in the record runs north, and Clay's letters spin it.
frus-1861-d297:
Seward heard from Mr. Harvey on 25 August 1861, in a dispatch sent from abroad. Congress received it as Document 297 in the papers printed with the President's message that year. It belongs to the first summer of the Civil War, when keeping Europe out of the war was a core task for Washington.

Readers get the field report side of the exchange, sent home for Seward to weigh and answer. For students of the war, the value lies in the sequence: one dated step in a long exchange. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1862-d97:
A State Department letter of 11 July 1862 told Charles Francis Adams what Washington wanted done. Congress received it as Document 97 in the foreign affairs volume that went with the President's message. The letter comes from the summer of 1862, the war's second year, a time when each foreign capital watched the war with care.

The text is Washington speaking: orders, guidance, and the facts the envoy was told to stress. Read in order with its neighbors, it shows diplomacy as daily work rather than grand speeches. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1862-d197:
Lord Lyons, the British minister in Washington, wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 16 December 1861, and the letter stands as Document 197 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. It came from the British legation a short walk from the State Department.

Lyons wrote while his government waited for Washington's answer in the Trent affair, the dispute over Confederate envoys seized from a British mail steamer. His manner was calm where London's first reaction had been fierce. Letters from his hand in this window show a minister trying to keep a quarrel from becoming a war. Britain's first concern in Washington was the blockade and what it cost British trade.
frus-1862-d297:
William H. Seward, as Secretary of State, wrote to William L. Dayton in Paris on 21 July 1862, in a dispatch printed as Document 297 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume.

Late July 1862 was the war's low summer for the Union: Richmond saved by Lee. A second Confederate army gathering, and calls in Europe to end the fighting by pressure. Seward's letters to Paris pushed back with facts and resolve. This dispatch shows the Secretary's method at its plainest, steady repetition of the Union's case to the court most likely to act. Edouard Thouvenel ran the French foreign ministry for most of 1862 and set Dayton's agenda there.
frus-1862-d397:
Two days after a companion instruction, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote again to Bayard Taylor in St. Petersburg, on 24 November 1862. The letter is Document 397 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed to accompany the President's annual message to Congress.

Short follow-up orders were the glue of Civil War diplomacy, since news crossed the Atlantic by ship and took weeks. Seward used them to correct, press, or calm his agents as events shifted. Paired with Taylor's own reports, this note helps a reader watch the Washington end of the Russian correspondence. In that quarter the Union enjoyed rare goodwill during the war.
frus-1862-d497:
On 26 April 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward sent this instruction to James Shepherd Pike, the American minister to the Netherlands. It is Document 497 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

Seward wrote on the day New Orleans fell to Farragut's fleet, the Union's greatest prize of the spring. News of that kind was diplomatic gold, and his orders abroad made the most of it. At The Hague the victory spoke to a trading people: the Mississippi was opening, and the Confederacy was shrinking. The instruction belongs to the confident late-April round of Seward's orders. In them he told his ministers, in effect, that the rebellion had passed its peak. Europe, he said, should take note.
frus-1862-d597:
Spain's minister of state wrote this instruction on 13 December 1861 to General Serrano, the captain general and governor of Cuba. It is Document 597 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, in an appendix of Spanish papers on Mexico.

Unlike most of the volume, this letter is not American at all: it is the Spanish government's own internal order, printed in translation. Cuba was the base and the prize of Spain's American policy, and Serrano commanded both the island and its part in the Mexican expedition. The document lets a reader see the allied move on Mexico from inside Madrid's chain of command, which is why the State Department preserved it.
frus-1862-d697: A Mr. Yrisarri wrote this dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 26 August 1862. The letter is document 697 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862, printed near the papers on Central America. The evidence names the writer and the date but does not state his post or his land, so this note claims no more than that.
frus-1863p1-d97:
Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Charles Francis Adams on 2 March 1863 — and wrote again, and again. Twelve letters to Adams in the volume bear this one date. Adams was the American minister in London. This letter is document 97 in part one of the 1863 volume, the first of the dozen.

A dozen sheets in a day is a desk cleared at one stroke, most likely a set of set-piece notes on the file's live points. Each stands on its own in the printing, numbered in line. This one opens the batch. Read as a group, the twelve show Seward putting the whole London brief in order on a single March day.
frus-1863p1-d197:
From Washington on 9 May 1863, Secretary of State William H. Seward sent this instruction toward London; the catalog title garbles the envoy's name as 'Mr. Adapts,' but the letter belongs to the run addressed to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It is document 197 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It is one of the papers the State Department later printed in its Foreign Relations series for 1863.

For readers today, these instructions reveal the thinking inside the State Department as clearly as any memoir. They show choices being made in real time, with poor information and high stakes. For a modern reader, it offers the war as working diplomats saw it: slow mail, sharp words, and constant risk.
frus-1863p1-d297:
An instruction dated 19 September 1863 went from Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, in London. It appears as document 297 of the 1863 diplomatic papers. It appears in the Foreign Relations series, where the State Department printed the papers it sent with the President's yearly message to Congress. It was one of 3 letters between the same men dated that day.

Confederate agents were buying ships and arms in Britain, and Washington wanted the trade stopped. Orders to London often carried protests, evidence, and legal arguments for Adams to use. It is a small piece of a huge correspondence, but the whole picture only emerges from pieces like this one.
frus-1863p1-d397:
To Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, Secretary of State William H. Seward sent this formal note on 23 February 1863. It appears as document 397 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It survives in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official record of its work abroad. It was one of 3 letters between the same men dated that day.

Canada, then a British colony, shared a long border with the Union. Worries about raids, plots, and smuggling across that line sit behind part of this correspondence. For a modern reader, it offers the war as working diplomats saw it: slow mail, sharp words, and constant risk.
frus-1863p1-d497:
Dated 7 May 1863, document 497 is a letter from Lord Lyons, the British minister in Washington to Secretary William H. Seward. It forms part of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official printed record of American diplomacy. The two men at the ends of this channel, Seward in Washington and Lyons speaking for Britain, wrote to each other almost daily.

The letter also shows the craft of the period: a few stiff phrases could carry a warning, and both sides knew how to read them. None of these letters worked alone. Read in sequence, they show two governments testing each other's limits while both, in the end, avoided a second war. That is the use of such a page: not a famous text, but a firm rung in the ladder of the record.
frus-1863p1-d597:
Document 597, dated 27 July 1863, records a letter from Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington to Secretary William H. Seward. The letter sits in the published record of how the Lincoln government handled foreign affairs in the summer of 1863. America was then in the third year of its Civil War, and every letter to or from London carried weight.

The standing business of this channel was friction at sea. Union warships stopped British merchant ships, and each seizure could spark a formal protest. The real subject under all the polite wording was British neutrality. Washington wanted it kept strict, and London wanted no quarrel it could avoid. Readers who work through the file in order will find this letter where the clerks of 1863 left it, in the middle of the stream.
plos-pbio-0020097:
Mark Jung-Beeman, Edward M. Bowden, Jason Haberman, and co-workers scanned brains during sudden insight for PLOS Biology in 2004. People solved word problems either by steady work or by a flash of insight, the classic aha moment. Brain imaging let the team compare the two routes.

The insight route lit up a distinct pattern, including an area tied to loose word links, just before the answer came. A burst of activity marked the moment the solution broke through. The study gives hard data on a mental event that feels instant and mysterious. It suggests insight is not magic but a real brain process that can be measured, timed, and perhaps trained.
plos-pbio-0020197:
Marcel Cardillo, Andy Purvis, Wes Sechrest, and a broad team assessed risk in the world's carnivores in PLOS Biology in 2004. They asked whether crowded human areas raise the extinction risk of meat-eating mammals like lions, wolves, and bears. Data covered species across the globe.

The team found that where people live densely, carnivores face higher risk, even after accounting for other traits like body size and range. Big predators need space, and dense human settlement eats that space. The result gives conservation a clear, testable driver to watch. It suggests that saving carnivores will depend as much on managing human spread as on guarding the animals themselves.
plos-pone-0000097:
Reijo Laaksonen, Mikko Katajamaa, Hannu Päivä, and a large team used systems biology to hunt drug side-effect markers in PLOS ONE in 2006. Some widely used drugs harm a small share of patients, and doctors cannot yet tell in advance who is at risk. The team studied a statin known to cause muscle problems in rare cases.

By reading genes, proteins, and blood chemistry together, they found pathways tied to the toxic response and candidate markers in plasma. A blood test that flags risk before harm starts would change how such drugs are prescribed. The strategy, reading the whole system at once, is the paper's lasting point, beyond the one drug studied.
plos-pone-0000197:
Jonas Binladen, M. Thomas P. Gilbert, Jonathan P. Bollback, and colleagues published this sequencing methods paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. The team used coded PCR primers, molecular barcodes attached during copying, so many samples could be sequenced at once by 454 parallel sequencing. That let them run high-throughput sequencing of multiple related gene copies in one batch.

Barcoding samples cut the cost of sequencing many specimens at once, a bottleneck in genetics at the time. The authors show the coded primer approach works on real amplification products. The trick became standard practice in the sequencing era that followed, from ancient DNA to microbiome studies.
plos-pone-0000297:
Barry Nicholls and Paul A. Racey published this bat study in PLOS ONE in 2007, posing a practical question in the title. Bats avoid radar installations, the authors report. That raises the idea that electromagnetic fields could deter bats from colliding with wind turbines, a growing cause of bat deaths.

Wind farms kill many bats, and a cheap deterrent would help both wildlife and operators. The authors document bats steering clear of radar and ask whether the effect can be borrowed. The paper links an odd behavioral observation to a real conservation technology problem.
plos-pone-0000397:
Naotaka Fujii, Sayaka Hihara, and Atsushi Iriki watched the monkey brain adapt during social interaction, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Neurons in the parietal cortex respond to movement, both one's own and others'. The team asked whether those motion-related neurons change their behavior as social situations unfold, a process they call dynamic social adaptation.

Reading others' movements is basic to social life: it underlies imitation, joint tasks, and judging intent. If single neurons adjust on the fly during interaction, the brain's social machinery is more flexible than a fixed wiring diagram suggests. The work helps connect brain cell activity to the give-and-take of real social behavior.
plos-pone-0000497:
Claudia Rodríguez-Almazán and colleagues found that unrelated proteins can help a folding protein succeed, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Proteins must fold from loose chains into exact shapes, and many fail and clump. The team showed that interactions with unrelated proteins increase the stability and formation of native proteins from unfolded monomers.

The result is counterintuitive: bystanders are usually expected to interfere, not assist. It suggests the crowded cell interior may actively support folding through weak, nonspecific contacts. That idea reframes how chemists think about making proteins in test tubes, where adding inert partner proteins might rescue yields of hard-to-fold products.
plos-pone-0000597:
Patric Hagmann and colleagues mapped the human brain's wiring as a network, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. They used diffusion MRI, which tracks water movement along nerve fibers. With it, they mapped human whole-brain structural networks. Those networks are the web of connections between brain regions in living people.

A structural network map is the scaffolding on which all brain activity runs. Network analysis reveals hubs and communities in that scaffolding, giving neuroscience a common map for comparing healthy and diseased brains. This paper was an early statement of the connectome idea, that the brain's connection pattern is itself a key to how it works.
plos-pone-0000697:
Heng Tao, Anthony J. Berno, David R. Cox and co-authors linked skin cell movement in a dish to gene variants, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Wound healing after injury to the epidermis remains hard to promote, partly because its factors are poorly understood. One essential step is re-epithelialization, where keratinocytes, the skin's main cells, migrate to cover the wound.

The title reports that migration rates in vitro are associated with SNPs in the KRT1 interval, a genome region named for a keratin gene. If inherited variants predict how fast skin cells crawl, healing speed may be partly written in DNA. That link could guide treatments for slow-healing wounds.
plos-pone-0000797:
Dev Churamani, Michael J. Boulware, Timothy J. Geach and colleagues characterized a new enzyme that makes calcium-releasing messengers, in PLOS ONE in 2007. ADP-ribosyl cyclases are remarkable enzymes able to catalyze several reactions. Among their products are cyclic ADP-ribose and NAADP, potent messengers that mobilize calcium inside cells. Not all cyclases, however, had been characterized at the molecular level.

Their subject is a novel intracellular cyclase, working inside the cell rather than on its surface. Characterizing it at molecular level means its sequence, its products, and how it is regulated. Calcium signals control everything from fertilization to secretion, so a new source enzyme redraws parts of that map.
plos-pone-0000897:
Thomas Webb and Robert Freckleton tested a classic size rule in animals where females are the larger sex, in PLOS ONE in 2007. In most species the sexes differ in size, and females are often bigger. Rensch's rule describes how that gap tends to change as species get larger overall.

Webb and Freckleton asked whether the rule holds when females lead in size. Their answer, flagged in the title, is that such species break the rule about half the time. A half kept rule is still useful, but it needs a better explanation. The study pushes biologists to ask what drives size gaps, not just describe them.
plos-pone-0000997:
Cheng Ding, Yan Liu, Yin Wang and colleagues found a brake on a special class of B cells, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. B1 B cells follow their own development path and do jobs distinct from standard B cells. What sets the size of that lineage was largely obscure.

Using mice that lack the Siglecg gene, marked with a glowing protein, the team show Siglecg limits the B1a branch. It does so by down regulating NFkappaB activation, a master switch for immune cell growth. A defined brake explains why this lineage stays a minority. It also gives immunology a handle for raising or lowering that population on purpose.
plos-pone-0001097:
Jason Slot and David Hibbett traced a nitrate eating gene cluster that jumped between fungi, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Some fungi carry a cluster of high affinity nitrate assimilation genes that switch on together. The cluster holds a transporter, a reductase and a related enzyme, a full kit for feeding on nitrate.

Using phylogenetic analysis, the pair present evidence the cluster moved by horizontal transfer between fungal lineages. A whole feeding kit moving at once can shift a species' ecology in one step. Their study ties that transfer to ecological transitions in fungi, changes in where and how species live. Gene clusters make such leaps visible.
plos-pone-0001197:
Age-related macular degeneration is the leading cause of blindness in the Western world, mainly affecting people over fifty. Peter Francis and colleagues studied variation in the complement factor H gene in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. That gene had repeatedly been shown to be a major factor in susceptibility to the advanced disease.

The authors examined haplotypes, the inherited blocks of variants in the gene. They checked their associations with drusen, the deposits that mark early disease, and with advanced macular degeneration. Sorting out which variant patterns raise risk sharpens genetic counseling and points at the complement system as a treatment target.
plos-pone-0001297:
DNA helicases are enzymes that unwind the double helix, a step required for repair, recombination, and replication. Sudha Sharma and Robert Brosh studied one human helicase, RECQ1, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Humans have five helicases of this family, several tied to diseases of premature aging and cancer risk.

The authors report that human RECQ1 responds to DNA damage. It is also required for resistance to genotoxic stress and for suppression of sister chromatid exchanges, a sign of faulty repair. Their work assigns concrete duties to the least-studied member of the family. It matters for understanding how cells guard their genomes.
plos-pone-0001397:
Yunfeng Li and colleagues published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on two proteins that uncouple energy use in cells. One protein, when raised, had been tied to weak insulin release. The other tends to drop in the muscle of people with type 2 diabetes. The team asked whether sugar drives these two proteins in unlike ways.

Working with insulin making cells of the pancreas, they tested how sugar levels shift each protein. The two did not move in step, which fit their hunch of opposed effects. The result helps clarify how fuel use is tuned in these cells. It may bear on why insulin release fails as diabetes takes hold.
plos-pone-0001497:
Jan Brascamp and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on how past views shape what we see now. When an image can be read two ways, sight flips between the reads. Shown at gaps, the image tends to return in the same read as before. The team asked how long that memory of a past read lasts.

They found the pull of past views works on more than one time scale at once. Both brief and longer spans shape the next read. That layered memory helps the brain settle vague input fast. It also shows past sight aids, rather than biases, clear seeing in many cases.
plos-pone-0001597:
Kristine Briedis, Ayelet Starr, and Philip Bourne published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on the human kinome, the full set of kinase enzymes. Kinases are prime drug targets, but some stay hidden when gene codes stray too far from known ones. Shape based searches can catch what code searches miss. The team ran such a search across the human set.

Their search found two kinases that code based hunts had missed. New kinases widen the list of druggable targets. They also show the known kinome was not yet closed. Each such find can seed a new drug line for cancer and other ills.
plos-pone-0001697:
Robert G. Wallace and Walter M. Fitch studied how bird flu crosses borders in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. The strain is highly pathogenic influenza A H5N1. Its geographic spread is a necessary step toward the virus evolving human-to-human spread. As it travels, it diversifies in response to local farming and social conditions.

The authors report that H5N1 immigration is filtered out at some international borders, meaning the virus fails to establish in certain countries it reaches. The full text gives the family-tree analysis of virus samples and the border patterns they found. Knowing which borders hold, and why, could help target surveillance where the virus is most likely to break through.
plos-pone-0001797:
Blerina Kola and co-authors studied how the hunger hormone ghrelin acts in the brain, in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Ghrelin and cannabinoids both stimulate appetite, possibly through the hypothalamic enzyme AMPK, a key regulator of appetite and metabolism. Rimonabant, a blocker of the cannabinoid CB1 receptor, can block ghrelin's hunger effect.

The team reports that ghrelin's hunger effect is mediated through central activation of the endogenous cannabinoid system. The full text gives the feeding experiments and the blocker tests. Two appetite systems acting as one pathway helps explain why CB1 blockers cut hunger so strongly, and why their side effects were so broad.
plos-pone-0001897:
Antoine Lutz and colleagues scanned the brains of meditators in a 2008 PLOS ONE study on compassion. Past scans had shown that two brain areas, the insula and the front cingulate, react when a person feels another's pain. What no one knew was whether training the mind to feel compassion on purpose would change that response.

The team used brain scans while skilled and new meditators heard sounds of people in distress. They compared how each group reacted as they held a kind, caring state of mind. The study tests whether long practice reshapes the brain's response to suffering. That bears on how mental training might aid care work and health.
plos-pone-0001997:
Alfredo Rodriguez and co-authors built a program that finds and sorts tiny knobs on nerve cells, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The knobs, dendritic spines, are where most excitatory synapses sit, and their shape is tied to learning and memory. Gauging their three-dimensional forms by hand was slow and imprecise, which blocked firm statistics.

Their software detects spines in fluorescence microscope images in three dimensions and classifies their shapes on its own. Fast, precise counts let labs compare spine types across health and disease. Such tools turn a craft task into data that large studies can trust.
plos-pone-0002097:
Karthik Jayapal and co-authors compared gene messages to proteins over time in a soil bacterium, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Streptomyces coelicolor is a model for the bacteria that make most of our antibiotics. Many biological processes are dynamic, with deep shifts at both the molecular and body level. Systems analyses profile either gene messages or proteins to watch them.

The team looked for genes where the two do not move together, divergent mRNA-protein dynamics. Where message and protein part ways, control must sit after the message is made. Such genes warn against reading gene activity as protein truth.
plos-pone-0002197:
Sophie Colomb and co-authors traced how two genes guide nerve growth in the fruit fly embryo, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. A hard problem in brain science is finding the cues that tell growing nerve fibers where to go. Those cues build the neat, repeated wiring of a nervous system.

In the fly, the genes Engrailed and Gooseberry-Neuro work together in a nerve cell called neuroblast 6-4. The team shows their joint action triggers the growth of the rear commissure bundles, bridges of fibers that cross the embryo. Small switches like these lay down the roads that whole brains are built from.
plos-pone-0002297:
Tomonori Takeuchi and co-authors studied a protein found only at one kind of synapse in the cerebellum, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. The cerebellum tunes movement. In its Purkinje cells, a protein called delphilin sits exactly at parallel fiber synapses. There it binds a glutamate receptor, GluR delta2, essential for long-term depression and motor learning.

Mice lacking delphilin let the team test its role head-on. They found both long-term depression, a lasting weakening of synapses, and the optokinetic response, a learned eye movement, were enhanced. An unusual result like this refines the model of how this region learns.
plos-pone-0002397:
Agudelo-Romero, working with fellow researchers, published a study in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names Patricia Agudelo-Romero, Pablo Carbonell, Miguel A. Perez-Amador, among others. Its subject is virus Adaptation by Manipulation of Host's Gene Expression. Viruses adapt to their hosts by evading defense mechanisms and taking over cellular metabolism for their own benefit.

Alterations in cell metabolism as well as side-effects of antiviral responses contribute to symptoms development and virulence. The piece walks readers through the question, the setup, and the steps that came next. The full text is free to read, so any reader can check the work and follow the links to past work.
plos-pone-0002497:
Dettenhofer and fellow authors published a research article through PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names Markus Dettenhofer, Fen Zhou, Philip Leder, among others. Its subject is formin 1-Isoform IV Deficient Cells Exhibit Defects in Cell Spreading and Focal Adhesion Formation. Regulation of the cytoskeleton is a central feature of cell migration.

The formin family of proteins controls the rate of actin nucleation at its barbed end. The paper sets out the problem first and then the line of work the team chose to take. That makes the article a clear record of one research question, the path taken to test it, and the limits the authors faced.
plos-pone-0002597:
Krach and co-authors published a research article in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names Sören Krach, Frank Hegel, Britta Wrede, among others. Its subject is can Machines Think? Interaction and Perspective Taking with Robots Investigated via fMRI. When our PC goes on strike again we tend to curse it as if it were a human being.

Why and under which circumstances do we attribute human-like properties to machines? The piece walks readers through the question, the setup, and the steps that came next. The result is a compact record of the work, of use to readers who study the same problem or teach it to others.
plos-pone-0002697:
In 2008, Miao Hao and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE. Their subject was Structure-Activity relationship and Substrate-Dependent phenomena in effects of ginsenosides on activities of Drug-Metabolizing P450 enzymes. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Miao Hao, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. Ginseng, a traditional herbal medicine, may interact with several co-administered drugs in clinical settings, and ginsenosides, the major active components of ginseng. Readers get a clear record of the question, the approach named in the abstract, and the context the authors give for the work.
plos-pone-0002797:
In 2008, Jianqiao Ge and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE about distinct neurocognitive strategies for comprehensions of human and artificial intelligence. The catalog record names Jianqiao Ge first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. Although humans have inevitably interacted with both human and artificial intelligence in real life situations. The piece stands as a short, open record of the research question and the grounds on which the authors pursued it. No results or figures are claimed in this summary beyond what the title and abstract themselves state.
plos-pone-0002897:
Darby Harris and Seth DeBolt measured how orderly plant cell walls are in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The wall is the main load-bearing frame of a plant and shapes growth, form, and defense against stress. Yet how its parts are built and adjusted was still not well understood at the level of mechanism.

Their topic was relative crystallinity, meaning how much of the wall material sits in neat crystal form. They studied how that trait is assembled and how plants adapt or adjust it. Growers and materials scientists both care, since wall structure affects crop strength and plant-based materials.
plos-pone-0002997:
Xiaomin Yu, Qing Zhou, Sung-Chou Li and co-authors catalogued silkworm microRNAs across development in 2008. MicroRNAs are tiny regulators that tune gene activity after genes are read, affecting development and metabolism. The silkworm Bombyx mori is both an industry animal and a model insect, and its genome had been sequenced.

Writing in PLOS ONE, the team describes the silkworm's microRNAs and how their expression changes across multiple developmental stages. Stage patterns hint at which growth steps each microRNA governs. The catalog supports silk biology and wider insect development research. The article appeared in PLOS ONE, an open access journal anyone can read free online.
plos-pone-0003097:
Qian-Jin Zhang, Xiao-Lin Li, David Wang and co-authors studied dendritic cells taking up tumor material by trogocytosis in 2008. Two parts of the antigen presentation pathway, TAP and MHC class I, are often deficient in tumor cells. Restoring them was shown to restore presentation, but tumors find other escapes.

Trogocytosis is nibbling membrane from another cell. The team reports it moves MHC-I peptide complexes from tumors and infected cells to dendritic cells, enhancing cross-priming and adaptive T cell responses. Published in PLOS ONE, that transfer could help vaccines work around tumor hiding. The article appeared in PLOS ONE, an open access journal anyone can read free online.
plos-pone-0003197:
Jonathan Livny, Hidayat Teonadi, Miron Livny and colleagues present a large-scale method to find bacterial small RNAs in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Diverse bacterial genomes encode many small non-coding RNAs, called sRNAs, that regulate a wide range of biological processes. Computer algorithms had proven effective at finding sRNA-encoding sites, but tools and infrastructure to run those computations at scale were lacking.

The team offer high-throughput, kingdom-wide prediction and annotation of bacterial non-coding RNAs. Readers get a pipeline meant to work across many species, not just one model bacterium. Broad coverage can reveal regulators that single-genome studies would never see.
plos-pone-0003297:
Yaron Ideses, Yifat Brill-Karniely, Lior Haviv and colleagues rebuild actin structures in the lab in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. During cellular migration, regulated actin assembly takes place at the cell leading edge, with steady breakup deeper in the cell interior. Actin polymerization at the plasma membrane pushes out cell protrusions such as lamellipodia and filopodia.

The title reports that the Arp2/3 branched actin network drives filopodia-like bundle formation in vitro. Readers see one network produce structures usually credited to another system. Rebuilding cell edges from parts helps settle how protrusions really form.
plos-pone-0007397:
Renaud Becquet, Ruth Bland, Valériane Leroy, and colleagues pooled data on breastfeeding and HIV transmission in 2009. Both breastfeeding pattern and duration are associated with postnatal HIV acquisition by infants. Their relative contributions had not been reliably quantified, leaving feeding advice for mothers with HIV uncertain in many low-resource settings.

The authors pool individual data from West and South African cohorts. In urban West Africa, stopping breastfeeding early was recommended, but exclusive breastfeeding was common. They separate effects of pattern from effects of duration. Their PLOS ONE analysis informs safer infant feeding guidance where formula is risky.
plos-pone-0007497:
Jyrki Selinummi and colleagues published a methods study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on automated analysis of cell images. Fluorescence microscopy is the standard tool for such work. It has real drawbacks: few usable color channels, overlapping dye signals, and added cost. The team asked whether ordinary bright field images could serve instead. Their test case was macrophages, immune cells often screened in large numbers.

Plain light images carried enough detail for the automated analysis. That means many screens may not need fluorescent dyes at all. Dropping the dyes makes large-scale cell work simpler and cheaper. It also avoids artifacts that staining can add. The study gives labs a leaner way to run image-based screens. A standard microscope method turns out to hold more information than its routine use suggests.
plos-pone-0007597:
Rohit Mehra and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on the bacterium that causes relapsing fever. Borrelia hermsii is a spirochete, a spiral-shaped bacterium, spread by ticks. It is famous for antigenic variation: it swaps its outer coat proteins to evade the immune system. Those coat proteins, called Vsps, come in many serotypes. The team examined the relation between each variant's structure and its function.

Different Vsp serotypes seem to do more than disguise the bacterium. Evidence suggests they also influence where in the body the bacteria settle. A coat that both hides the germ and steers it is a double tool. Mapping which structures go with which behaviors helps explain the waves of fever. Each relapse follows a coat change, so the coat catalog is central to the disease. The study connects protein shape to the bacterium's strategy.
plos-pone-0007697:
Andre Sousa and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It concerns a gene variant tied to diabetes and heart disease. The gene is called TCF7L2, and one variant, named rs7903146, has been linked again and again to type 2 diabetes. Diabetes in turn raises the risk of coronary artery disease.

The team asked whether that variant also tracks how severe heart disease becomes and whether patients survive. They report that it does. A variant known for diabetes may therefore also help flag which heart patients face the greatest danger.
plos-pone-0007797:
Mariangela Chisari and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It watches how G proteins behave when a cell's receptors are stimulated. G proteins relay signals from receptors to the cell's machinery. The team measured an effector enzyme, phospholipase C-beta, as it responded.

Sensors tracked the making of two messenger molecules in living cells. The results show that G protein subunits split apart after stimulation. They also move to new places inside the cell. Both the split and the move shape the cell's answer. Signaling is thus a matter of travel as well as chemistry.
plos-pone-0007897:
Santina Bruzzone and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It tests a metabolic drug in a mouse model of multiple sclerosis. The model, EAE, mimics the immune attack that strips nerve insulation. Activated T lymphocytes drive that attack.

The drug blocks Nampt, an enzyme cells need to make NAD, a core energy molecule. Blocking it in activated T cells caused catastrophic NAD depletion. Treated mice showed less demyelination and less disability. The approach turns an energy dependency into a weakness. It suggests a new angle for treating autoimmune disease.
plos-pone-0007997:
Alfredo Castello and colleagues showed how the AIDS virus quiets a host cell in PLOS ONE in 2009. HIV carries a cutting enzyme, a protease, that snips viral proteins into shape. The team found it also snips two host proteins the cell needs to start making its own proteins.

With those start factors cut, the cell's normal protein making stalls, while the virus can still push its own agenda. The sabotage helps the virus take over the cell's workshop. Blocking the cut is hard without harming the drug targets already in use, but the step is now clearly mapped.
plos-pone-0008097:
Hui Zhu and Andrew Bendall studied a gene that tells cartilage cells when to swell and harden in PLOS ONE in 2009. Bones grow by first laying down cartilage, then swapping it for bone. The gene, Dlx5, works inside the cartilage cells themselves.

In mice, Dlx5 drove that swelling step, and it could also cover the job of its sibling gene Dlx6 when that gene was missing. A backup that truly works is a gift to the growing skeleton. The finding helps explain why some gene faults spare the bones they were expected to harm.
plos-pone-0008197:
Jennifer MacKellar, Samuel W. Cushman, and Vipul Periwal described waves of fat growth in a PLOS ONE paper from 2010. When mammals eat more calories than they burn, the surplus is stored mainly as fat. Steady excess requires fat tissue to enlarge over time. Faulty fat growth may be a key factor in insulin resistance.

The team studied the genetically obese Zucker fatty rat. They tracked how its fat tissue expands in waves rather than smoothly. Knowing the timing of growth helps explain when tissue takes in new cells. It also frames how obesity develops in this widely used model.
plos-pone-0008297:
Zoltan Beck and colleagues studied red blood cells and HIV in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. CD4 cells are the major target of HIV infection in blood. Claims that HIV-1 also binds red blood cells had generated controversy. The Duffy blood group antigen was proposed as the binding site. Binding without complement proteins was part of the dispute.

The team examined the question directly with infectious virus. Human erythrocytes selectively bound and enriched infectious HIV-1 virions. If red cells carry virus, they could shape how HIV spreads in the body. The finding reopens a debated part of HIV biology.
plos-pone-0008397:
Fa-Xing Yu and Yan Luo studied gene regulation by glucose in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Thioredoxin interacting protein, or Txnip, is a multifunctional protein. It helps regulate the cell cycle and cellular metabolism. Its expression is induced by glucose, adenosine-containing molecules, and other cues. The underlying regulatory mechanism was not fully known.

The team found tandem ChoRE and CCAAT motifs control Txnip expression. These DNA motifs and their associated factors respond to glucose or adenosine signals. Pinpointing the switches explains how diet-related cues tune this gene. That bears on diabetes and metabolism research.
plos-pone-0008497:
Alyssa Barry and co-authors analyze malaria vaccine targets in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Plasmodium falciparum causes the most deadly form of human malaria. Its antigens vary greatly, which blocks a broadly effective vaccine. Yet population genetics has rarely guided vaccine design. The team study genes for ten leading vaccine-candidate antigens. They gather data across parasite populations in a meta-analysis.

They find the population structures of those genes contrast sharply. Some antigens vary by place, others are more uniform. Vaccine design should account for those patterns. A vaccine built on a variable antigen may fail where strains differ most.
plos-pone-0008597:
Oliver Niehuis and co-authors study DNA swapping in a parasitoid wasp in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. The swapping, called recombination, occurs in most species that reproduce sexually. Yet its gains for evolution remain elusive. Past work in the honeybee found a very high rate of swapping genome-wide. The wasp Nasonia is a relative with a distinct breeding system. Males hatch from unfertilized eggs in that system.

The team measure the swapping rate across the wasp genome. They assess how it shapes genome structure over time. A contrast with the honeybee tests if high rates are shared in this insect group. The work adds a key case to a long debate.
plos-pone-0008697:
Lukas Vrba, Taylor Jensen, James Garbe, and colleagues asked how two small RNAs get switched off. Their cancer study ran in PLOS ONE in 2010. The RNAs, miR-200c and miR-141, help cells keep a tidy, sheet-like form. When cells lose them, they can loosen and spread, a step toward worse cancer. Something must silence them in tumor cells.

The team checked DNA methylation, a chemical tag that often mutes genes. Healthy and cancer cells showed matching tag patterns near these RNAs. Heavy tagging lined up with low RNA levels. Finding the off switch suggests drugs that strip such tags might restore control.
plos-pone-0008797:
Minli Xu and Zhengchang Su built a faster way to compare gene switch patterns. Their methods paper appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Transcription factors bind DNA at sites described by frequency tables. Scientists often search databases for similar binding patterns. They also group patterns into families. Old comparison methods first align the patterns, which can distort short ones.

Their new method compares patterns without any alignment step. Tests showed it matches similar motifs and separates different ones well. Skipping alignment speeds large database searches. Gene regulation studies can now cluster thousands of motifs more cleanly.
plos-pone-0008897:
Asako Shindo, Yusuke Hara, Takamasa Yamamoto, and colleagues showed frog embryo cells need a calcium surge to line up correctly. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. During gastrulation, frog tissues fold and stream in coordinated ways. Each cell needs a clear internal direction, called polarity. Neighboring tissues interacting can trigger signals inside cells. Calcium spikes were the suspected trigger here.

When tissues touched, calcium rose inside the responding cells. Blocking that rise prevented proper polarization. Direction is thus set by a neighbor-triggered calcium signal. The mechanism helps explain how embryos organize their first great movements.
plos-pone-0008997:
Guillermo Solovey and Silvina Ponce Dawson modelled how calcium signals spread inside cells, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Calcium is a messenger cells use for a huge range of tasks. Its messages vary in space and time, from small blips to waves. Much of the calcium enters through channels called IP3 receptors, grouped in clusters.

The model follows calcium release spreading from channel to channel within a cluster. That percolation-style spread explains why signals can stay tiny or ignite fully. Small changes in the cluster tip the balance between the two outcomes. The maths helps make sense of calcium signals seen under the microscope.
plos-pone-0009097:
Matthias Mueller and co-authors profiled the surface spikes of many bird flu types in the lab, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Hemagglutinin, the HA spike, is how flu viruses grab cells. Research had concentrated on the dangerous H5 and H7 subtypes. But bird flu mutates and reshuffles so fast that other subtypes matter too.

The team made HA proteins from several avian influenza subtypes. They characterised how antibodies recognise each version. A broader library helps test kits spot whichever subtype appears. Preparedness improves when diagnostics are not built for two subtypes only.
plos-pone-0009197:
Dana Gwinn, John Asara, and Reuben Shaw published this cell division study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Cells must enter and exit division in the right order, or copies go wrong. A web of signals times each step, backed by checkpoints that halt mistakes. The study focuses on raptor, a protein that helps control cell growth.

The authors report that raptor gains a phosphate tag during mitosis, the stage when chromosomes split. The tag is added by cdc2, a master enzyme that drives cells into division. That link ties the growth-control machinery directly to the division clock. It helps explain how cells coordinate growing in size with splitting in two.
plos-pone-0009297:
Hai Yu and co-authors published this hepatitis B study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Hepatitis B virus comes in several genotypes, labeled by letters. A strain called W29, taken from patients in northwestern China, did not fit the known set. Related odd strains had also turned up in Vietnam and Laos.

Using family tree and distance analyses, the team grouped these strains together. They propose the cluster forms an additional genotype, named I. Adding a genotype is not bookkeeping for its own sake. Genotypes differ in how disease progresses and how treatment works, so a missed one can mislead doctors in the regions where it circulates.
plos-pone-0011397:
Dan Yan and colleagues reported in 2010 a way to make radiation kill tumors more effectively. Radiation breaks tumor DNA, but cancer cells survive by repairing the breaks quickly. Two repair proteins do much of that work, and the team used a small RNA molecule to lower both at once inside tumor cells.

With the repair proteins reduced, tumors became far more sensitive to radiation in their tests. The strategy turns the cancer's own defense into a liability, so lower radiation doses might do the work of higher ones. That matters because radiation harms healthy tissue too. If the approach holds up in further testing, patients could gain stronger tumor control with fewer side effects. The paper offers a clear, testable route toward kinder and stronger radiotherapy.
plos-pone-0011497:
Xinwen Liang and co-authors traced in 2010 how one repair gene produces many different protein forms in mammals. The gene makes MsrB1, an enzyme that repairs proteins damaged by oxidation. Its diversity comes from two tricks: intronization, in which new introns are born inside the gene, and later processing that trims the protein into varied final forms.

Together those tricks let a single gene supply a whole toolkit of related repair enzymes with different traits. Such variety shows how mammals expand their defenses without adding new genes. For protein science, the case is a lesson in economy: evolution edits the script and the staging, not just the cast. Understanding how the forms differ may matter for aging research, since repair of oxidized protein is one of the maintenance jobs that falter with age.
plos-pone-0011597:
Benedetta Leuner, Erica Glasper and Elizabeth Gould studied sex, stress and brain growth in rats for PLOS ONE in 2010. Stress usually harms the hippocampus, a brain area tied to memory and mood. Stress hormones rise, new neuron growth slows, and cell branches shrink, changes linked to anxiety and low mood.

Sexual experience also raises stress hormones at first, so the team expected harm. Instead, repeated mating boosted new neuron growth in the hippocampus once the early hormone spike passed. The result shows that not all stress-like states damage the brain, and that rewarding experience can leave the brain better supplied with fresh cells.
plos-pone-0011697:
Anita Palepu and co-authors followed injection drug users in Vancouver, Canada, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Unstable housing and homelessness are widespread in this group, and the two problems feed each other. The team asked whether entering addiction treatment was linked to gaining stable housing over time.

Using prospective cohort data, they examined the treatment-housing link while tracking participants forward. Their findings bear on whether recovery programmes should treat housing as a core outcome rather than a side issue. For services, the evidence supports joining addiction care with housing support instead of tackling either alone.
plos-pone-0011797:
Roopa Nalam, Claudia Andreu-Vieyra and Martin Matzuk studied support cells of sperm production in mice, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Sertoli cells nurse developing sperm and are governed by several nuclear factors, including the retinoblastoma tumour suppressor protein. The authors hypothesised this protein mediates tumour formation in mice lacking inhibin alpha, a known Sertoli regulator.

Removing both inhibin alpha and the retinoblastoma protein led to early Sertoli cell dysfunction. The double loss reveals a partnership behind healthy sperm care. It also helps explain how Sertoli tumours arise when these guardians fail together.
plos-pone-0011897:
Luis López and co-workers tested in 2010 how best to treat skin cells that cannot make enough coenzyme Q10. This compound carries electrons in the cell's energy system and also acts as an antioxidant. Cells lacking it, taken from patients, offer a test bed for supplements such as ubiquinone, related CoQ compounds, and vitamin C.

The treatments did not all act alike: effects depended on which compound was used and how long the cells were exposed. Some analogs helped energy production while others diverged, a caution against treating all CoQ products as interchangeable. For patients whose illness rests on CoQ10 shortage, those time and compound details shape what a sensible supplement plan looks like.
plos-pone-0011997:
Ellouise Leadbeater and co-workers studied in 2010 paper wasps in which many helpers raise young that are not their relatives. In the wasp Polistes dominulus, nearly a third of co-foundresses are unrelated to the dominant female whose offspring they help rear. Helpers usually gain through family ties, so unrelated help is a puzzle.

The study asks whether helping is tailored toward direct fitness: gains the helper itself can bank, such as inheriting the nest. If unrelated helpers profit directly, their behavior is less altruistic than it looks. The wasps thus test a general rule of social evolution, that apparent selflessness usually hides a payoff somewhere.
plos-pone-0012097:
Yousef Jamali, Mohammad Azimi, and Mohammad Mofrad built a computer model of living cells for PLOS ONE in 2010. Real cells are soft, springy, and full of inner parts, and how they respond to push and pull helps them form tissues with the right shapes. Testing those responses in the lab is hard, so a good model lets researchers ask questions they cannot easily test on real cells.

Their model treats the cell as a soft material with inner structure, then watches how a whole group of cells behaves under force. It can show how single-cell stiffness adds up to the strength of a tissue sheet. Such models help explain how tissues hold their form, and how that form can fail in disease.
plos-pone-0012197:
Sara Alvarez, Javier Suela, Ana Valencia, and co-authors profiled chemical silencing marks in adult leukemia for PLOS ONE in 2010. In acute myeloid leukemia, cancer cells often shut genes off by coating them with methyl groups, a change that leaves the DNA letters untouched. Some patients also carry large chromosome rearrangements, and how the two kinds of change relate was not settled.

The team compared methylation patterns with each patient's chromosome status and outlook. If certain silencing patterns line up with certain rearrangements, they may refine prognosis beyond either test alone. They may also predict who benefits from drugs that strip methylation away, a therapy that helps only some patients today.
plos-pone-0012297:
Jinnuo Han, Perminder Sachdev, and Kuldip Sidhu combined two strategies to reprogram human body cells, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Turning an ordinary cell back toward a flexible, stem-like state had been achieved several ways, but usually by inserting foreign material, and usually in very few cells. Chemical and small-molecule treatments were already known to help the process along.

Their combined approach pairs an epigenetic treatment, one that loosens the chemical locks on genes, with a non-genetic method. Higher reprogramming rates without inserted genes would make patient-specific cells safer for therapy and easier to produce for research. Each gain in efficiency brings lab-grown replacement tissues a step closer to practical use.
plos-pone-0012397:
Peter Chen, Kristin Willner, Amy Butani and colleagues showed that rapid genome reading can spot engineered changes in the anthrax bacterium, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. The 2001 anthrax letter attacks proved the need to identify biothreat germs fast and to tell apart strains that look nearly identical. Slow lab methods leave investigators guessing during an outbreak.

Using 454 pyrosequencing, the team drafted whole genomes quickly and picked out genetic modifications. Fast drafts let analysts spot insertions and swaps that mark a lab-made strain. The approach strengthens biodefense and outbreak tracing, where hours matter and a missed change can mislead the whole response.
plos-pone-0012497:
Vishal Patel, Gurkan Bebek, John Mariadason and colleagues predicted and tested gene networks behind intestinal cancer, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Colorectal cancer grows through stacked mutations, and a few driver genes give cells their growth edge. Most drivers are known, but the networks they disturb are not, and those networks decide how a tumor behaves.

The team used computation to predict which network links the drivers rewire, then tested the predictions in cells. Confirmed links become candidate drug targets that single-gene thinking misses. The predict-then-test loop is a practical template for turning cancer genome lists into treatment ideas.
plos-pone-0012597:
Lee and colleagues used computer models to study a bacterial protein called Obg, found in Bacillus subtilis. Obg belongs to a family of proteins that bind GTP, a small energy-carrying molecule. The protein has two parts that stay much the same across species, one that grips GTP and one rich in the amino acid glycine.

Their 2010 modelling study maps how Obg meets the nucleotides it binds, atom by atom in a virtual model. Knowing the shape of that grip helps explain what Obg does inside the cell. It also gives other researchers a base for tests on this whole protein family.
plos-pone-0012697:
Larsen, Lelic, Parsons and co-authors used a computer method to predict which virus pieces killer T cells can see. West Nile virus is a growing public health threat, and vaccines need targets the immune system recognises. Their 2010 study applied reverse immunology, scanning the virus's full protein with the NetCTL prediction tool.

The scan listed likely CD8 T cell epitopes, the short pieces shown to killer cells. Shortlists like this cut years of lab testing down to the best candidates. The same approach speeds vaccine work on many viruses.  Predicted pieces were ranked for follow-up laboratory testing.
pmc-4580597:
Paradis, Ben, Denson, and their colleagues reviewed racism as a determinant of health in 2015. A growing body of population studies had documented health impacts of racism in recent years. That evidence had not yet been gathered into one comprehensive meta-analysis on racism itself.

The team systematically reviewed the literature and pooled results across studies. Their synthesis weighs how strongly racism is linked to poorer mental and physical health. A pooled estimate gives policy makers a firmer base than scattered single studies. The review supports treating racism as a public health issue that shapes illness and access to care.
pmc-5075697:
Rognes, Flouri, Nichols, and their colleagues presented VSEARCH in 2016, a versatile open source tool for metagenomics. VSEARCH processes and prepares nucleotide sequence data for metagenomics, genomics, and population genomics. It is multithreaded and free of charge, with its source code open to all.

The tool was designed as an alternative to USEARCH, a widely used program whose source code was not open. Open code lets researchers inspect, fix, and extend the methods they rely on. VSEARCH covers clustering, searching, and quality steps needed before analysis. It became a core free tool for labs profiling microbial communities.
pmc-7005297:
Lei Yang, Peng Shi, Gaofeng Zhao, and coauthors reviewed targeting cancer stem cell pathways in 2020. Cancer stem cells were first found in leukemia in the mid nineteen nineties. These cells can renew themselves and seed new tumor growth.

They are blamed for relapse, spread, and resistance to standard therapy. The review covers the main signaling pathways that keep such cells alive, including Wnt, Notch, and Hedgehog. Drugs aimed at those pathways are surveyed with their trial results. Killing the bulk of a tumor may not cure it if this root population survives.
pmc-7334197:
Konrad Karczewski and a very large team of co-authors published in 2020 a map of which human genes can tolerate change and which cannot. They built it from genetic variation gathered in more than one hundred forty thousand people. Where a gene almost never shows damaging changes in healthy people, that absence itself is evidence the gene does essential work.

The authors turn those patterns into a spectrum of constraint, a graded measure for gene after gene across the genome. Doctors and researchers use such measures to judge whether a rare change found in a patient is likely to cause disease. The work became a standard reference for reading human genomes in clinics and in studies of inherited illness.
pmc-8500697:
Damian Santomauro and collaborators estimated in 2021 how much the COVID-19 pandemic raised the global burden of depression and anxiety during 2020. Even before the pandemic, these two disorders were among the leading causes of health related burden worldwide. The pandemic then created conditions, from isolation to economic shock, that damage mental health on a vast scale.

The team combined data on infection rates and restrictions with surveys of symptoms, covering more than two hundred countries and territories. They calculate the extra cases of major depression and anxiety attributable to the pandemic's first year, and where the increases fell hardest. Their figures helped governments grasp that the mental health costs of the crisis rivaled many direct effects of the virus.
pmc-8728197:
Jan Meier-Kolthoff and co-authors described in 2021 a paired pair of databases built for naming and classifying bacteria and archaea from their genomes. Microbial classification now leans heavily on genome data, while the number of named species and their sequences keeps climbing steeply. Keeping names, classifications, and sequences in step has become a real challenge for database builders.

Their two resources work as a tandem: one computes a genome based classification, the other maintains the official naming record for prokaryotes. Together they let a researcher place a new genome quickly and check that its name follows the rules. The article explains how the pairing stays accurate as public repositories grow.
plos-pone-0357597:
Shuang An, Dan-ni Gu, He-jun Huang, Jun-qiang Luo, and Rong-rong Liu wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article about tourism in Tianshui, China. It models tourist loyalty, the choice to return or recommend a place. Three forces are built into the model: how crowded the place feels, what social value visitors think the trip gives them, and how good they judge the service to be.

The method is structural equation modeling, which tests how several influences act on each other at once. Crowding can sour a trip even when service is good, and the model weighs that tension. Destination managers in Tianshui and other growing Chinese tourist cities can use the results to balance visitor numbers against experience.
plos-pone-0350497:
Stephanie Colwell, Prabhakar Chalise, Byron Gajewski, Isuru Ratnayake, and Dinesh Mudaranthakam published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It models count time series data that depend on place, such as case counts recorded across regions over time. The models used are COM-Poisson INGARCH models, statistical tools built for counts that bunch or spread unusually.

Spatially dependent counts appear in disease surveillance and crime statistics, where one area's numbers sway its neighbors'. A model that respects that dependence gives truer forecasts and alarms. Biostatisticians and public health analysts tracking outbreaks across counties are the readers for this modeling work.
plos-pone-0359197:
Kateřina Abrhámová, Alexandra Gredová, Karolína Navrátilová, Mohamed Boumaiza, and Petr Folk wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on yeast genetics. It studies the intronic RNA of RPL22 paralogs, copies of a ribosomal protein gene, and reports that this RNA acts as an allosteric switch, a molecule whose binding changes a protein's behavior.

Introns were long treated as waste cut out of genes, so finding a working switch among them changes how yeast gene control is pictured. Paralogs are near-duplicate genes, and cross-talk between them can fine-tune protein production. Molecular biologists studying gene regulation are the readers for this small RNA with an outsized job.

europmc-pmc7026697: This 2019 research paper covers the global, local, and national burden of colorectal (of the colon and rectum) cancer and its attributable risk factors in 195 countries. Data about the global, local, and country-specific variations in the levels and trends of colorectal (of the colon and rectum). Solid numbers like these help health officials aim prevention money and effort where they count most.
