memoirs-of-the-court-of-st-cloud-being-s: This St. Cloud volume treats the ambitious imperial family. Napoleon's grasping brothers and sisters reach eagerly for thrones. The shrewd letters note their pride and their quarrels. A family raised too high and too fast.
plos-pone-0358797:
Sarah Alexandra Marshall leads a team of six asking what a health program for low income Black men with chronic illness would need to succeed, in PLOS ONE in 2026. The group studied is underserved in the southern United States, and one proposal on the table uses a universal basic income to open access to care. Before any launch, the researchers interviewed thirty-one interest holders, including men from the target population, about conditions such an intervention must respect.

Five themes emerged. The men typically delay seeking care. Relationships are strained by incarceration and poverty. Prison health services and ordinary healthcare are not built to help them. Community level barriers pile up. Racism and poverty are intertwined and entrenched. The authors argue any fair intervention, income based or not, must work at individual, family, community, and institutional levels at once, or it will fail the very people it names.
plos-pone-0358597:
Yueyi Tan leads a team of six using machine learning to map how two kinds of shops compete for space in Shenzhen, China, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Convenience stores run light, cheap, and everywhere; supermarkets and malls are capital heavy and choosy. The team fed geospatial data and measures of how people perceive streets into a stack of interpretive models that can reveal bends and interactions, not just straight line effects.

The two formats followed distinct locational logics. Convenience stores spread widely and reacted strongly to nearby competition, to the proximity of everyday services, and to how a place feels to pedestrians. The big formats clustered where returns justify their cost. Untangling which urban features pull each format helps planners zone commercial districts deliberately, and helps chains pick sites with their eyes open about which game they are playing.
plos-pone-0351697:
Ahmed Tarfy leads a team of eight publishing the protocol for a first in human trial of a personalized cell therapy in advanced colorectal cancer, in PLOS ONE in 2026. The treatment harvests T cells from the lymph nodes that drain a patient's tumor. Those nodes have already met the cancer. Their cells can be trained in the laboratory against the patient's own tumor mutations. Sequencing and prediction software select the targets. The trained cells return as a living drug.

The trial unfolds in three parts: collecting nodes and manufacturing the cells, a single infusion after immune conditioning chemotherapy, and follow up stretching to five years. Up to sixteen patients with stage four disease can join. Being a protocol, the paper promises no results; its value is transparency about how a bespoke therapy is built and judged. Safety at this stage outranks cure, and the staged design reflects that caution.
plos-pone-0357497:
M. Arunadevi and colleagues published a 2026 engineering paper in PLOS ONE on a common manufacturing defect: layers splitting apart when glass-fiber composite panels are drilled. Delamination weakens the finished part, and it depends in tangled ways on drill shape, size, speed, and feed. The team ran a full grid of drilling trials on glass-fiber laminates, photographed the damage, and trained a neural network that also had the physics of cracking built into its learning rules.

The physics-informed network predicted the damage measure very accurately on held-out trials. Feed rate mattered most, followed by laminate thickness and drill diameter, while faster spindle speeds actually reduced damage by cutting more cleanly and pushing less. Interactions mattered too, especially between feed and speed. Adding the physics constraints made predictions sturdier and better at generalizing. The authors offer the model as a planning aid for shops that drill composite parts.
plos-pone-0356997:
Kathleen O'Connor and coauthors published a 2026 genomics study in PLOS ONE on a quiet kind of variation in Staphylococcus aureus, a bacterium behind many skin and hospital infections. Genes can spell the same protein with different codons, and bacteria prefer some spellings, affecting how much protein gets made. The team measured codon bias across thousands of genes in a reference strain and compared it with all public complete genomes of the species, sorted by disease, institution, and site.

Bias varied gene by gene and isolate by isolate. Ribosome machinery genes showed the strongest, most consistent bias everywhere, suggesting heavy pressure to keep them highly expressed. One hospital's genomes, from Nairobi, stood out as most different. In a well-known strain, higher bias scores did tend to mean more protein in culture. Silent spelling choices, they say, are a real layer of this pathogen's diversity that evolution studies have largely skipped.
plos-pone-0357797:
Veronika Frybortova and coauthors published a 2026 mouse study in PLOS ONE on whether a ketogenic diet changes how the body handles ozanimod, a drug used in multiple sclerosis. High-fat, very-low-carbohydrate diets are being explored alongside MS therapy, but diets can retune the liver enzymes clearing drugs. Female mice ate a normal or ketogenic diet for four weeks; the team then measured metabolism, gut microbes, liver enzymes, and the drug's path through the body.

The diet produced the expected ketosis, raised blood cholesterol, and reshaped gut microbial communities, while most other measures moved only modestly. Liver enzyme activity shifted both ways: one family sped up, another slowed, and a third trended down. Drug exposure in ketogenic mice ran somewhat higher, though the difference was not statistically firm. The signal is small, they say, but real enough that diet-drug interactions deserve attention as the therapy spreads.
plos-pone-0356197:
Yan Zhao and coauthors published a 2026 study in PLOS ONE grading how well hospitals across China's thirty-one provinces turned resources into care between 2019 and 2023. They combined a three-stage efficiency model that strips out outside influences, a dynamic index tracking change over time, and a spatial statistic that tests whether efficient provinces cluster together.

Average efficiency sat below the ideal frontier, leaving real room for improvement, though the trend rose over the five years. Stripping out those advantages lowered scores, showing that good conditions had propped some provinces up, and the regional ranking reshuffled: the center briefly passed the east, while the west trailed throughout. Technical progress, not better management alone, was the main brake on output growth. Efficient provinces clustered stably below the Yangtze River, while low-efficiency clusters mostly dissolved by 2023, suggesting catch-up. The map is offered as guidance for national hospital reform.
plos-pone-0353797:
David Bellini and co-authors report a 2026 study of how men feel about heat therapy before and after trying it. Heat therapy here means sitting in hot water, a habit linked in past research to lower heart disease risk. Twenty young, active men took a one-hour soak in warm water and answered custom surveys just before and just after the session.

Most men expected the soak to feel easy and calming, and many still found it pleasant, yet half said it was harder and less fun than they had guessed. Given a free choice, they would have stayed in for about half the set time. Heat and time demands, the authors argue, may keep people from using a therapy that could help them.
plos-pone-0341397:
Taoqing Liu and Yaqin Ren survey more than eight hundred physical education undergraduates in Guangdong, China, about how satisfied they are with the courses meant to make them teachers. Their framework ties six features of course design to three basic student needs drawn from a well-known motivation theory. The survey compared two related majors and probed which course gains best predict overall satisfaction.

Overall satisfaction sat at a moderate level. Teaching-focused majors rated course goals, knowledge gains, and skill building higher than sports-training majors, who were also far less keen to teach after graduating. Knowledge and skill gains correlated most strongly with satisfaction. Liu and Ren argue that programs should rebuild courses around what students feel they truly gain, especially for majors drifting away from teaching.
plos-pone-0355997:
Shinhyun Kim and colleagues ran a computer-based hunt for new drug candidates that mimic risperidone, a medicine that blocks dopamine D2 receptors, but stay out of the brain. Their 2026 study starts from a quirk of such drugs: raising the hormone prolactin outside the brain may protect nerve cells, while brain exposure causes sedation and movement side effects.

Starting from four hundred look-alike molecules, the team filtered for ones predicted not to cross into the brain, then docked the survivors against the receptor in simulation. Eight beat risperidone's docking score, four kept the key contacts inside the receptor, and one stayed most stable in motion simulations. The shortlist now awaits real lab testing, which the authors stress has not yet happened.
plos-pone-0355197:
Satoshi Kondo and colleagues surveyed 630 Japanese citizens about a proposed answer to doctor shortages: letting hospital paramedics take on more medical tasks. Their 2026 study measured the public's general trust in hospital paramedics and their acceptance of specific procedures, then repeated the questions after a short educational briefing about the paramedics' role.

Trust and acceptance started high and stayed high. The briefing nudged acceptance of paramedic procedures up slightly but did not move general trust, which the authors suspect already rests on confidence in ordinary ambulance paramedics. For policymakers, the results suggest the public is not the obstacle to task shifting; building credible certification and training systems is the work that remains.
plos-pone-0356797:
Chaoqun He and Racidon P Bernarte surveyed six hundred Chinese livestream shoppers. Half were young digital natives, and half were older adults. The survey asked what makes them buy again from a live commerce host. Their 2026 study modeled three facets of service quality. They were the host's professionalism, the interactive experience, and after-sales support. Trust served as the middleman. Generation was the dial that turns each effect.

All three facets built trust, and trust fed intentions to return. But the generations weighted them differently. Older shoppers leaned hardest on professionalism and after-sales care. The young prized interactivity. The authors advise platforms to segment their playbook. They suggest certifying hosts for older audiences. For the young, they suggest investing in interactive features, even augmented reality try-ons.
plos-pone-0356497:
Kinza Shahid and colleagues produced the largest protein catalogue yet for Fasciola gigantica, a liver fluke of buffalo and cattle that also infects people. They worked from adult worms taken from naturally infected buffaloes in Punjab, Pakistan. Their 2026 proteomics study separated the fluke's proteins. It verified them by antibody blotting and identified them by mass spectrometry. The focus was the proteins the parasite secretes into its host.

Nearly five thousand proteins were catalogued, including a large set of predicted secreted ones. The functional profile leaned heavily on enzymes that cut, dissolve, and oxidize. That is the toolkit of a parasite that burrows through tissue and feeds on its host. A further slice tied to immune manipulation. Each such protein is a candidate target for drugs or vaccines against a costly livestock disease.
plos-pone-0355697:
Tomoki Sakaguchi and three colleagues compare the spores of four fission yeast species under the microscope, in this 2026 study. Fission yeasts are workhorse organisms for cell biology, and the best-known species makes spores with a distinctive bumpy coat tied to toughness. Whether its relatives share that design was unknown. The team imaged spores from all four species with light and electron microscopy, then stress-tested them.

Surface structures differed sharply between species. The fibrous coat and the dense outer layer seen in the famous species were largely missing from the other three. Its spores also survived heat and alcohol best. The authors conclude that each fission yeast evolved its own spore architecture, possibly tuned to its habitat, a reminder that even close relatives solve the survival problem differently.
plos-pone-0356597:
Eric Pelzl and four colleagues study a well-known Mandarin sound change inside real conversation, in this 2026 experiment. When two low tones follow each other, the first traditionally rises, becoming indistinguishable from a genuine rising tone, a puzzle called third tone sandhi. Ten pairs of native speakers played a phrase-matching game. One read a phrase aloud and the other picked it from a screen, under conditions that did or did not trigger the change.

The setup produced real confusion exactly where the sound change predicted it. Pairs coped mainly by keeping the first low tone lower toward its end, effectively avoiding the full change and preserving the contrast. The authors say even a tightly structured game can reveal how speakers steer around ambiguity, a first step toward understanding how this rule behaves in everyday talk.
plos-pone-0354797:
Michael Meece and four colleagues test light therapy on injured fruit fly eyes in this 2026 study, carefully varying the dose. Shining near-infrared light on tissue, called photobiomodulation, is proposed to aid healing, but studies use such different settings that results rarely compare. The team damaged fly retinas with light, then treated the flies twice daily for ten days at two wavelengths and four total doses.

One wavelength clearly helped: at 850 nanometers, photoreceptor function recovered better, and stronger doses worked better still. The other wavelength, 950 nanometers, produced no real recovery at any dose, apart from a hint of benefit at one middle dose. Energy molecule levels rose under some treatments but did not line up neatly with recovery, suggesting several processes are at play. The authors say wavelength choice matters as much as dose.
plos-pone-0356697:
Xingyue Pu and Zhigang Zhong track whether China's cancer hospital beds are shared fairly, using fifteen years of national statistics in this 2026 study. Oncology beds grew steadily from 2008 to 2022, though growth slowed. The authors measured fairness two ways, against population and against land area, using standard inequality tools that also separate disparities within regions from those between them.

Judged by population, bed allocation was quite equal and improved over the period. Judged by geography, it was severely unequal throughout, with no improvement, meaning patients in sparse regions face long journeys regardless of headcounts. Most inequality in both views came from within regions rather than between them. The authors argue policy should now chase geographic accessibility and local balance, to ease the notorious difficulty cancer patients face getting admitted.
plos-pone-0353997:
Yuanyuan Dai and colleagues built a faster way to measure how pear flesh bends and flows under pressure. Such measurements matter for sorting, packing, and shipping fruit without bruising it. Their 2026 study combined squash tests on Huangguan pears with computer models of the tissue and a machine learning system.

The learning system acted as a stand-in for slow physics simulations, reading spatial patterns and sequences in the test data. A tuned genetic search then picked the tissue values that best matched real squash tests. Errors stayed very small compared with the lab measurements. Dai and colleagues say the approach cuts the need for destructive testing and can guide gentler fruit handling equipment.
plos-pone-0354497:
Tope Olubodun and co-authors reviewed published cases of stomach paralysis linked to a popular class of diabetes and weight-loss drugs. These medicines, called GLP-1 receptor agonists, commonly slow the gut, but full gastroparesis is less recognised. Their 2026 systematic review searched four databases for real-world reports through late 2025.

Only twelve reports covering thirteen patients met the review's rules. Most patients were women with type 2 diabetes, though some had no diabetes. Semaglutide appeared most often, and symptoms began anywhere from hours to months after starting, often after a dose rise or careless restart. The authors urge clinicians to watch for the condition and to record cases carefully, since evidence remains thin.
plos-pone-0328697:
Neha Kardam and Denise Wilson compared computer methods that sort short student comments into themes. Universities collect thousands of brief feedback answers, and reading them all by hand is impractical. Their 2026 study used engineering students' expectations about support from teachers, assistants, and peers, gathered over several years.

Five topic models, from classic statistical methods to a modern language-model approach, were run on the same cleaned comments. The team judged them by theme coherence and by checks beyond machine scores, addressing a gap in earlier comparisons. Their aim is practical guidance: which method to use, when, and with what caution. Done well, such sorting can steer teaching support toward what students actually ask for.
plos-pone-0355397:
Isaac Faustino and co-authors checked whether children in state protective custody face more forceful interventions in emergency departments. They studied thousands of behavioural health visits by children between 2021 and 2023. Their 2026 analysis compared children in protective custody, children with a new report filed, and children with no involvement.

Children in custody received sedating injections and physical restraints more often than the other groups. By three days into the visit window, about one in six had received an injection, well above the other groups. Adjusted models confirmed a higher risk rate for custody children. Faustino and colleagues argue the gap demands scrutiny of how departments care for the most vulnerable children in crisis.
plos-pone-0355597:
Baoguo Luo and co-authors built a machine learning shortcut for judging whether bridges can safely carry permitted overweight vehicles amid normal traffic. Such vehicles need official authorisation, and full engineering simulation of every crossing is far too slow. Their 2026 framework learns from a detailed grillage model of bridge behaviour under mixed traffic.

The model predicts how much the heavy vehicle amplifies load effects compared with ordinary traffic alone. Training data came from systematic runs of the high-fidelity simulation, which captures how loads spread across the deck. The learned surrogate then answers in a fraction of the time. Luo and colleagues aim the tool at permit offices facing rising volumes of exceptional loads.
plos-pone-0355497:
Mirinae Kim and Young-Hoon Park ask in 2026 whether bleeding inside the eye in advanced diabetic eye disease follows the seasons. They reviewed several thousand affected eyes seen at a Seoul hospital over three years and compared monthly bleeding rates with weather records. Pressure inside the eye before and at bleeding was also checked.

Bleeding peaked in late spring and early summer. Temperature, humidity, and rain did not explain the pattern in their models. Eye pressure at bleeding differed from pressure at the prior cold season visit, hinting that pressure shifts or seasonal blood sugar changes may play a part. More study is needed, the authors say.
plos-pone-0355297:
Pingping Xie, Jinfa Gu, and Jie Huang pool in 2026 trials of neuromuscular training for young male tennis players, covering power, speed, and skill drills. Earlier reviews mixed groups and lumped outcomes together, blurring what helps. Their search kept controlled trials of healthy male players and split outcomes such as stroke speed, serve accuracy, sprint, jump, and agility.

Training favoured stroke speed, short sprint, jump height, agility, and serve accuracy in pooled results, but not placement accuracy. Certainty was low or very low for every outcome. No single drill type is proven, the authors warn, and better trials with longer follow up are needed.
plos-pone-0354297:
Kazi Afaq Ahmed and three colleagues published this 2026 study of investment risk in Pakistan, built around the Altman Z-score, a long-used formula that flags firms heading toward distress. They combined company traits, economic conditions, and political stability into an investment risk index and tested what drives it.

Firm traits, the wider economy, and politics all moved risk significantly, and larger firms surprisingly carried more of it. Fixed asset buildup and tax expenses also mattered. Ahmed offers the index as a structured diagnostic for investors, with lessons that may travel to other developing economies.
plos-pone-0354897:
Karar Zunaid Ahsan and four colleagues published this 2026 study of fairness in mothers' health care in Bangladesh. They linked national surveys of mothers and health facilities across 2001, 2010, and 2016. They asked whether gaps between poor and non-poor women in pregnancy care, facility births, and complication treatment closed faster where clinics were better prepared.

Overall use rose, yet poor and non-poor gaps persisted and sometimes widened, especially for giving birth in facilities. Ahsan concludes that upgrading clinics alone does not deliver fairness, and policy must target the women still left behind.
plos-pone-0354997:
Subina Bajracharya, Sadikshya Neupane, and Parita Shrestha published this 2026 community study of a simpler way to spot overweight children in Bharatpur, Nepal. Body mass index needs proper scales, height boards, and trained staff, which large school screenings often lack. The team measured three hundred children aged six to eleven, comparing neck size with standard body measures.

Neck circumference tracked the established measures closely and identified overweight children with useful accuracy, and the authors derived cutoff values for local use. Bajracharya presents the tape-around-the-neck check as cheap, quick screening for schools with few resources.
plos-pone-0354097:
Wang and colleagues, in a 2026 review and data study, search blood gene data for markers tied to how proteins are tagged and edited after they are built. Such edits, called posttranslational modifications, help control protein behavior, and their failure is suspected in Parkinson's disease. The team hoped to find a few genes that flag the disease or suggest treatment targets.

Starting from hundreds of genes that differed between patients and healthy people, the team kept only those tied to protein editing, then let machine learning rank them. Three genes passed checks for diagnostic value and were all turned down in patients. Further analysis linked the gene set to immune signaling, and patients showed fewer of several active immune cell types. The team also mapped the genes and screened compounds that might act on them. They present the three genes as candidate blood markers, pending wet-lab proof.
plos-pone-0354597:
Kanoksing and colleagues, in a 2026 study, look for gene variants that shape the pattern of asthma in adults. One form of asthma is driven by a set of immune signals that raise certain white blood cells and narrow the airways over time. The team genotyped one hundred twenty-five patients and measured their lung function, blood cells, and immune signals.

Two variants stood out. One in the IL5 gene tracked strongly with high levels of eosinophils, a white cell type tied to allergic inflammation, and with weaker lung function. Each extra copy of the risk letter added to the effect. A variant in the IL13 gene tracked with more of the helper cells that drive this inflammation and with a higher risk of fixed airflow blockage. Other variants showed smaller links. The authors suggest gene tests could one day help sort asthma patients for targeted treatments.
plos-pone-0353197:
Goldschmidt and colleagues, in a 2026 study, grow three cell lines from a benign but stubborn jaw tumor of dogs, called canine acanthomatous ameloblastoma. Living cell lines let researchers test treatments in dishes before animals. The lines were grown from naturally occurring tumors, confirmed as dog and as surface-type cells, and read at DNA and RNA level.

The lines kept their parent tumors' mutations, including a change in a growth gene found in every sample, and shared a set of other mutations in most lines. Their gene activity matched the known fingerprint of this tumor from earlier studies and clustered far from healthy gum tissue. Growth programs linked to invasion and several signaling pathways stayed switched on in the dish. The authors say careful profiling, including where lines drift from their tumors, is what makes them trustworthy stand-ins for pre-clinical testing.
plos-pone-0350097:
Xudong Gao, Jiying Shang, and Yu Song test a way of strengthening ageing concrete frames with tensioned cables, in this 2026 PLOS ONE engineering study. Buildings lose load-bearing strength over decades, creating safety risks. External cables can push back against sagging, but most research strengthens only the beams. This team reinforced beams and columns together and loaded a single frame until it yielded.

As the cables' sag increased, the frame's weakest zone moved away from the beam ends toward the joints, and peak strain fell sharply — by roughly seventy percent in their best case. Carrying capacity and yield load both rose with cable sag and more stirrup steel. Fuller reinforcement, they argue, buys old frames a safer second life.
plos-pone-0353697:
Daniel Sanin-Villa and four colleagues write the day-ahead timetable for a small local power grid, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. Their microgrid mixes wind turbines with batteries, and the challenge is deciding each hour what to generate, store, or draw, while wasting as little energy and emitting as little carbon as possible. Batteries do the balancing: soaking up surplus wind, covering calm spells, and steadying voltage.

Their genetic-algorithm scheduler was tested against two established optimisation methods under identical conditions, on two standard test networks of different sizes, in both connected and islanded modes. Careful scheduling matters because every wasted kilowatt in a microgrid is a larger share of the whole than in a national system.
plos-pone-0352897:
Johanna Stähler and five colleagues test a hopeful idea — that training makes effort itself feel more valuable — and find it wanting, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. Sixty-two young adults were assigned to eight weeks of high-intensity jump training or a control condition. Before and after, they pedalled a laboratory bike, sometimes at set intensities and sometimes choosing their own, while rating how effort felt and wearing brain scanners.

Nothing moved: not self-reported effort value, not willingness to work harder, not the brain signals. Statistical analysis favoured the null result rather than merely failing to find an effect. The value of effort, the authors suggest, may be a stubborn trait that a single training block cannot rewrite.
plos-pone-0353397:
Wohnrade and colleagues tested sound-wave scanning as a marker of nerve disease in mice in a 2026 study. The disease studied slowly kills the nerve cells that move muscles, and trials lack easy ways to track its course. Mice bred to develop a similar illness had their leg nerves and muscles scanned over time.

Scans picked up nerve shrinkage and muscle wasting at the same time as, or earlier than, standard nerve tests and movement checks. Scan changes also matched tissue damage seen under the microscope. A painless scan that tracks disease this closely could help test new drugs in animals first, and it may later guide similar tracking in people.
plos-pone-0352397:
Al-Tameemi and colleagues set out a trial plan in 2026 on a fruit fiber supplement for fatty liver disease. The disease, tied to body metabolism, is now the leading cause of long-term liver trouble worldwide. Thirty adults in Nottingham will take either the fiber, called pectin, or a dummy supplement for six weeks, with neither side knowing which.

Blood, stool, and body measures will be taken before and after to track inflammation, gut microbes, and metabolic health. Gut changes are a prime suspect in how fiber might calm the liver. A small careful trial like this tests both benefit and practicality before a larger study is funded.
plos-pone-0350397:
Tessone and colleagues piloted a new tear-film camera at a specialist eye center in a 2026 study. Dry eye is common, yet its signs and symptoms often disagree. The camera measures the oily top layer and the watery layer beneath it at extremely fine detail, in adults with and without dry eye signs.

Eyes with clinical signs of dry eye had a clearly thinner oily layer than eyes without signs. Symptom scores from a standard questionnaire were gathered for comparison as well. A thin oily layer lets tears evaporate faster, so measuring it directly could sharpen diagnosis. The small pilot supports larger studies of camera-guided dry eye care.
plos-pone-0341997:
Gambin and colleagues set out a trial plan in 2026 to validate a driving-based sleepiness test. Daytime sleepiness causes many road crashes, yet the standard lab test watches people lie still, which poorly matches driving. Their simulator version judges wakefulness during a driving task instead.

Fifty-four people will take both tests in random order: patients with sleep apnea after stopping or continuing their night therapy for a week, plus healthy controls. Stopping therapy briefly brings back sleepiness in a controlled way. If the simulator test matches the standard while feeling more like real driving, licensing decisions could rest on fairer evidence.
plos-pone-0350897:
Rafaela de Almeida and seven colleagues report this 2026 PLOS One clinical trial comparing a laser treatment against daily eye drops for glaucoma and high eye pressure. Thirty patients took part, and in each person one eye received the Pascal-pattern laser treatment while the other eye used travoprost drops, after a washout period. Pressure in both eyes was tracked for a year, including peak pressure during a water-drinking test.

For most of the year the two approaches lowered pressure by similar amounts, and by twelve months the laser-treated eyes averaged slightly lower pressure than the drop-treated eyes. Vision tests showed no meaningful difference or progression in either group. The authors say the laser matched a standard daily drop, which matters for patients who struggle with lifelong medication routines.
plos-pone-0352997:
Lin Ruan and seven colleagues present this 2026 PLOS One laboratory study of a new weapon against drug-resistant urinary tract infections. The bacteria behind most such infections increasingly shrug off first-line antibiotics. The team tested a membrane-attacking compound called COE-D8 against ninety-three clinical samples of uropathogenic E. coli, most of which resisted standard drugs at high doses.

Nearly all the samples stayed sensitive to the new compound, which killed bacteria several times faster than standard antibiotics by tearing their membranes. Because the compound alone can harm host cells, the team paired it with the antibiotic fosfomycin, which lowered the needed dose and doubled survival in a mouse safety model. Bacteria also struggled to evolve resistance, supporting the pair as a candidate for stubborn infections.
plos-pone-0350697:
Joseph Shearer and colleagues checked whether heart failure risk scores built from blood proteins travel well between different kinds of studies. Three published scores, each built in a different setting, one community cohort, one trial, and one registry, were all tested in the same community group. Each score sums many proteins measured on the same platform into one number meant to forecast death.

All three scores predicted death over five years, and each held up after accounting for standard clinical measures. The scores overlapped only moderately, yet they agreed on a small set of proteins, with renin in all three. Calibration, whether predicted risk matched real outcomes, was strong. The practical message is reassuring: a protein score built in one population is not trapped there, and protein panels add information doctors can use beyond the usual chart.
plos-pone-0352197:
Nathan Yu and colleagues tested twelve machine learning tools on a question about young drinkers. How early can a drinking pattern forecast the drinker someone becomes? The subjects were adolescent mice, and the drinking records were simulated from published mouse work. Long real records are scarce, so simulation filled the gap. The team fed each tool the record cut at growing lengths. That mimics a researcher deciding when a forecast can be trusted.

Six tools classified the final drinking paths with outstanding accuracy. They were near perfect by the end of the record and already strong at its midpoint. Four more tools did acceptably, and two lagged behind. The ranking gives addiction researchers a practical shortlist. It also shows how much observation an early, reliable signal costs.
plos-pone-0329197:
Judging diabetes care quality from the patient's seat requires a questionnaire that makes sense in local language and culture. Yohannes Mulu Ferede and colleagues translated a widely used chronic care survey into Ethiopian use and checked it carefully, in this 2026 PLOS One study at referral hospitals in the Amhara region.

Patients with type 2 diabetes answered the twenty-six questions, which cover five habits of good chronic care, in face-to-face interviews during spring 2025. Experts rated each question's relevance, and statistical checks tested whether answers grouped as expected and stayed consistent. The adapted tool gives Ethiopian clinics a validated way to hear how coordinated and supportive their diabetes care feels.
plos-pone-0344697:
Kabiru Ahmed and colleagues propose a fresh maths method for solving sets of linked equations that must stay inside a set of allowed values. Such problems show up in engineering and science models. Their method updates a good guess step by step, restarts when stuck, and tunes two dials by a rule that keeps the update well behaved.

Proofs show the method reaches a solution from any start, and do so without a strict smoothness demand that older proofs needed. That weaker demand widens the problems the proof covers. Tests against known methods on sample problems ran well. For users, the gain is a solver that is steadier on hard, constrained equation sets.
plos-pone-0351497:
Paula Hage Boutros and colleagues followed more than six hundred pregnant women across Lebanon to learn what shapes a babys birth weight. A Mediterranean style diet has been tied to healthier births, yet its role for babies born small or large for their stage was unclear. Diet, weight gain, blood pressure, mood, and background factors were tracked across pregnancy.

Babies of mothers who followed the local Mediterranean pattern most often landed in the healthy middle weight band. Single foods mattered in finer cuts: dairy linked with lower middle weights, dried fruit with higher ones. Steady weight gain guarded against small babies, while higher blood pressure raised small baby risk. Large babies tied to prior large births, more past births, and poor late sleep.
plos-pone-0350297:
Setor K Sorkpor and colleagues surveyed one hundred and seventy adults living with HIV in Ghanas Volta Region about shame, mood, food access, and views on daily HIV drugs. Strong drugs work only when taken steadily, yet inner shame can sour beliefs about treatment. Models tested whether low mood carries that effect, and whether hunger changes its strength.

Inner shame linked with more negative beliefs and attitudes toward the drugs. Low mood carried a clear share of that link. Hunger sharpened the path from shame to low mood, so indirect harm ran stronger where food was scarce. Care that treats mood and food need together, the authors argue, may protect drug adherence better than pills alone.
plos-pone-0349597:
Huiping Lai and colleagues tested an added breathing routine for older adults with stable long term lung disease. Fifty one patients were split by chance. Both groups did whole body breathing exercise daily for three months. Half also added a cycle technique that loosens mucus through controlled breaths, huffs, and coughs, for thirty minutes a day.

Added training lifted one key lung flow measure, stretched six minute walk distance by about twenty metres beyond controls, and lowered breathlessness and overall symptom scores. Life quality marks also favoured the added routine. A cheap, drug free breathing cycle, practised daily, can give older lung patients a real functional gain.
plos-pone-0348197:
Changning Ren and co-authors surveyed social media users in 2026 about when health posts by bloggers get adopted as guidance. Bloggers now shape health behaviour strongly, and the trust mechanics behind that influence needed a model.

More than twelve hundred people answered a structured survey. Perceived blogger competence changed how information quality and credibility flowed through usefulness into adoption. In short, competent seeming bloggers make good information land harder, and weak seeming ones waste it. The model helps health agencies choose partners for campaigns: expertise must be visible, not merely real, to move public behaviour.
plos-pone-0348097:
Béatrice Parguel, Marine Agogué, and Julie Gauneau ran two laboratory experiments on a double-edged question: what happens when women researchers appear more often in science media? Women remain undercovered relative to men. Their 2026 experiments showed members of the public and graduate students a simulated science newsletter with varied gender balance, then measured beliefs about ability, expertise, and academic careers.

Seeing more women researchers narrowed the gap between men's and women's confidence in their own ability in both groups. The public also rated women researchers as more expert, though graduate students did not shift on that point. Unexpectedly, male graduate students found academic careers less attractive when visibility rose. The authors draw lessons for universities and media about handling representation with care.
plos-pone-0349697:
Hassan A Aljaberi, Saeed Rahmani, and Humam H Alrikabi reviewed records of more than two thousand Iraqi children to map how eyesight errors align with crossed or wandering eyes. Their 2026 study covered three specialist children's eye centers, comparing just over a thousand children with horizontal eye misalignment against a larger group without it, all measured with drops that relax focusing.

Inward-turning eyes came with strong farsightedness in most cases and appeared at younger ages. Outward-turning eyes leaned the other way, toward nearsightedness and astigmatism. Statistical modeling confirmed moderate to high farsightedness as a powerful predictor of the inward type, and nearsightedness with astigmatism of the outward type. The authors support early focusing checks for any child suspected of misalignment, since glasses alone can change the course.
plos-pone-0349797:
Chunyan Wang and colleagues ran large laboratory tests on strengthening sand with bacteria that deposit calcium carbonate, a natural cement. The open question was how the shape of the grouting pipe changes the treatment. They compared a standard straight pipe with a new spiral design across several injection setups in big sand columns.

Pipe design strongly shaped how far the cement spread and how even it was. A single injection pipe with one extraction point strengthened only a narrow zone around it. Setups with three injection points, and the spiral pipe, treated a much wider radius. For engineers, the message is that delivery hardware matters as much as the bacteria themselves.
plos-pone-0350197:
Adam Sundh and colleagues checked whether a one-leg hamstring strength test gives the same numbers when athletes repeat it on different days. Thirty college male athletes performed maximal pushes in a long-lever bridge position, heels on force plates, across three sessions. The team measured peak force and how fast force rose in the first fractions of a second.

Peak force proved steady between sessions, and early force measures were moderately to well consistent, though noisier. Small differences between sessions were mostly trivial. Coaches use such tests to track hamstring recovery and injury risk, so knowing the measurement error matters. A change bigger than that error band is likely real progress, not test wobble.
plos-pone-0349197:
Lewis D Taylor and colleagues fed Atlantic salmon extra vitamin D for six months and then read which genes switched on or off in the fish's skin. Skin is a salmon's first shield against the germs that plague fish farms, and vitamin D is known to shape immunity in other animals. So the team asked whether diet could tune that shield.

About one hundred and fifty genes changed with the diet, and a good share of them govern inflammation and the ways skin cells flag invaders to the immune system. The pattern pointed to calmer inflammation alongside stronger early defences. The authors suggest that getting vitamin D levels right in feed could help farmed salmon resist skin disease, a costly problem for the industry and for fish welfare.
plos-pone-0348497:
Antonio Pérez-Torres and co-authors present a method for spotting gearbox damage early, before a failing gear stops an industrial line. Their system listens to vibration signals, chops them into short windows, and sums up each window with measures from both the raw signal and its frequency pattern. A statistical method then compresses those measures and watches for drift away from healthy behaviour.

Tested on recorded data spanning different loads, speeds, and levels of wear, the method proved sensitive to slow, progressive damage and flagged faults while they were still in early stages. Two control statistics did the judging, separating normal running from failure conditions cleanly. The authors offer the approach as a practical tool for planned maintenance in plants where a breakdown is especially costly.
plos-pone-0348697:
Nima Kianfar and co-authors reviewed sixty-one studies on how ordinary people help track and control diseases spread by mosquitoes. Official surveillance is costly and patchy, while phone apps and backyard reporting can widen coverage cheaply. The team searched five major databases across a quarter century and catalogued how each project recruited helpers, checked their data, and used the results.

Most studies appeared after twenty seventeen and clustered in Europe and the Americas, with very few in Asia. Malaria drew the most attention, then dengue, and most projects ran in cities. The authors find citizen science a genuine complement to official systems, while warning that bias in who reports, and uneven data checking, still limit how far the results can be trusted.
plos-pone-0349297:
Yinghong Li and colleagues charted head and neck cancers across five East Asian countries from nineteen ninety to twenty twenty-three, using the latest global burden estimates. They covered China, Japan, both Koreas, and Mongolia, tracking new cases, deaths, and lost healthy years, then projected trends forward to twenty thirty-eight. Smoking was examined as the leading suspected driver.

The five countries split sharply. China and Mongolia improved on both new cases and deaths, South Korea held cases steady while deaths dropped, but Japan and North Korea worsened on both measures. Patients everywhere skewed older over time, and smoking stayed the dominant risk factor. Forecasts see Japan and North Korea still rising. The authors argue that tobacco control remains the region's biggest lever against these cancers.
plos-pone-0349397:
Yi Wang and colleagues reviewed scans from two hundred and forty-five men whose prostate cancer blood marker rose again after surgery, a sign the cancer may be back. All received a modern tracer scan that lights up prostate cancer cells wherever they hide. The team recorded how often the scan found disease at each blood marker level and where the spots appeared.

The scan found at least one lesion in three quarters of the men. Detection climbed from just over half at the lowest marker levels to about nine in ten at the highest. Verified cases showed a pelvis-first pattern, with most disease in the surgical bed or nearby lymph nodes. Blood marker level, tumour grade, and how fast the marker doubled predicted a positive scan. The authors offer benchmarks to guide targeted salvage treatment.
plos-pone-0349097:
Isabel T Held and colleagues piloted a tiny implanted port that lets researchers drip medicine into a mouse's middle ear again and again without repeated surgery. The device answers a practical problem in hearing research: drugs meant to rescue faulty proteins in genetic deafness must reach the inner ear regularly. The human route under study runs through the middle ear. They adapted a button implant already used for blood vessel access.

Mice carrying a mutation that mimics a human deafness syndrome, and normal littermates, received the implant on one side only. Over four weeks the animals behaved and balanced normally, saline injections through the port ran smoothly for two weeks, and hearing was not significantly harmed. The authors call the approach feasible and offer it as a stand-in for testing ear tube delivery in people.
plos-pone-0348597:
Jong-Hyun Kim presents a fast way to simulate balloons on a computer, complete with inflation, deflation, and the spin a real balloon gives when air rushes in or out. Full fluid simulation is far too heavy for games or virtual reality. His method instead pushes the balloon's surface points around under simple constraints, adds reaction forces borrowed from airflow physics, and weights those forces by distance travelled along the surface.

Rotation is handled in one whole-body step rather than vertex by vertex, keeping the maths cheap. Tests on meshes of many shapes and weight distributions ran in real time even at high detail, while still showing recognisable balloon behaviours such as bulging and twisting recoil. Kim targets interactive uses, from games to virtual product demos, where plausible motion matters more than laboratory accuracy.
plos-pone-0348797:
Satoru Iwata, Yumi Miura, and Takashi Iwamoto show a virus-free way to rearrange chromosomes inside a living mouse tissue. Big DNA swaps help scientists study how the genome is built and repaired, but virus delivery is slow and needs special labs. Their 2026 study uses electric pulses to push gene-editing tools into the lining of the mouse uterus.

The pulses produced the intended swaps between chromosomes at several sites. A very large flipped segment was also repaired with the help of a small donor template. Deep sequencing confirmed the new joins letter by letter, though changed cells were few, as expected. The shortcut gives labs a quicker, cleaner stage for studying DNA repair in the body.
plos-pone-0346097:
Sabrina Hepner and co-workers compare the scattered side genomes, called plasmids, of the bacteria that cause Lyme disease. These bacteria carry many loose DNA circles and lines besides their main chromosome, and the mix varies wildly. Their 2026 study assembles eighty-six genomes across most known species in the group, thirty of them newly read, and counts and sorts every plasmid.

Each strain carried anywhere from a handful to more than twenty plasmids. Only two plasmids appeared in every strain. Species tied to rodents carried more plasmids than those tied to birds. Swapping and reshuffling looked constant, including for the system the bacteria use to dodge immunity. The loose genome may help these bacteria adapt to many hosts.
plos-pone-0347997:
Naomi Assame, Susan Greenhalgh, John Tingle, and Gillian Yeowell reviewed the laws and policies meant to help England's National Health Service respond when patients are harmed by their treatment. Searching medical and legal databases and grey sources from 2000 to 2025, the 2026 scoping review charted one hundred twenty-one records and synthesised them thematically, the first exercise of its kind.

The review found statute, policy, and stated NHS values pulling in different directions yet depending on each other. Most strikingly, workplace culture seemed to outweigh written rules in deciding how providers actually respond to harm. The authors call for research on how law and policy might shape that culture for the better.
plos-pone-0346497:
Ethan Shaw, Suraj Chandramouli, and Michael Dzakovich present a kit of hydroponics parts that anyone can make on a home 3D printer, in this 2026 PLOS ONE paper. Hydroponics grows plants in water instead of soil and gives tight control over growing conditions, but ready-made systems can be costly and hard to adapt.

The printed pieces snap together into a vertical tower with one or two columns and adjustable height, so the setup fits a classroom, greenhouse, or growth chamber. As a check, the team grew spinach under different salt levels and got results matching a standard deep-water system. They pitch the kit as a cheap, flexible option for research and teaching.
plos-pone-0347697:
Anna Khoperia and colleagues review seven years of liver cancer in Georgia, the Caucasus country that launched a national hepatitis C elimination program in 2015, in this 2026 PLOS ONE paper. Hepatitis C is a leading cause of hepatocellular carcinoma, so the team linked cancer, death, and treatment registries for cases diagnosed through 2022.

More than seventeen hundred cases appeared, mostly men around their early sixties, and two-thirds arrived at late stages; most patients had died by the end of follow-up. Screening of cancer patients for hepatitis C rose from rare to nearly universal, and over half of those tested carried the virus. The data show both the program's reach and how much cancer burden remains.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
For the first time, the Council said the words two states out loud for Israel and Palestine. On 12 March 2002, it adopted Resolution 1397. Fourteen members voted yes and none voted no. Syria held back. The vote came amid the bloodshed of the Second Intifada.

The text backs a vision of the region with two states side by side. Israel and Palestine would live within safe, agreed borders. It demands an instant halt to all acts of violence. Terror, goading, and wrecking all count. It calls on both sides to work the Tenet plan and the Mitchell Report. Those steps aimed to restart talks on a final deal. The two-state phrase became standard diplomatic language.

One of the UN's first disarmament bodies died by this single sentence. The Commission for Conventional Armaments had been created in the UN's early years. It worked on plans for limiting armies and non-nuclear weapons. By 1952 the General Assembly had judged the effort stalled. Its resolution of 11 January 1952 pointed the way out.

Resolution 97, adopted on 30 January 1952, dissolves the Commission outright. It follows the Assembly's recommendation, cited in the text. No debate details survive in the record. The move closed a chapter of early Cold War arms talks. Disarmament work shifted to new forums. The Council had helped launch the Commission's work in 1949; five years on, it signed the body's end.

The Yugoslavia war crimes tribunal faced a staffing snag in 2005. Too few candidates had been nominated as temporary trial judges. Those judges, called ad litem judges, were also barred from re-election. Their first terms expired on 11 June 2005. Resolution 1597, adopted unanimously on 20 April 2005, rewrote the rules.

Acting under Chapter VII, members amended the tribunal's statute. Serving temporary judges could now stand for re-election. The nomination deadline gained thirty extra days. The annex spells out the election system. The Assembly elects twenty-seven judges from a Council list. Each serves four-year terms. The fix kept trials staffed as the Hague court worked through its remaining cases.

Qatar ended its status as a British-protected state in September 1971. Oil had made the small Gulf peninsula rich. Independence brought a swift UN application. Resolution 297 was adopted unanimously on 15 September 1971. The Council acted at its 1578th meeting, less than two weeks after independence.

The members recommended Qatar's admission to the General Assembly. The Assembly seated Qatar within the week. Gulf neighbors Bahrain and Oman joined the UN the same season. Together they shifted the region's diplomacy away from London. For Qatar, membership was the legal seal on sovereignty. The one-sentence text hides a busy year in which Britain's Gulf treaties all came to an end.

Resolution 197, adopted unanimously on 30 October 1964, recommends the Republic of Zambia for membership in the United Nations. Zambia had been independent for just six days, having ended British rule as Northern Rhodesia on 24 October. Its application reached the Council almost immediately.

The whole text is the recommendation itself, addressed to the General Assembly, which holds the final vote on admissions but can act only after the Council speaks. Zambia's quick admission reflected the speed of decolonization in Africa during the 1960s, when new states joined the UN in rapid succession. The landlocked copper-producing country in southern Africa has kept its seat ever since.

Local elections in the Democratic Republic of the Congo are the focus of Resolution 1797, adopted on 30 January 2008. Congo had held landmark national polls in 2006 after its transition, and local elections were the next unfinished layer of the peace settlement. The Secretary-General had recommended that the UN mission, MONUC, help organize them.

The Council authorized MONUC to assist the Congolese authorities, including the national electoral commission, with organizing, preparing, and running the local polls. The work was to be done working closely with world partners and the UN country team. The resolution treats elections as central to restoring peace, reconciliation, and the rule of law after years of war.

Liberia's civil war draws an armed response in Resolution 1497, adopted on 1 August 2003 by twelve votes to none with three abstentions. Fighting had produced a humanitarian disaster in Monrovia and was destabilizing the region. A ceasefire signed at Accra in June was not holding on its own, and West African leaders, led by Ghana and Nigeria, were preparing to send troops.

The Council authorized a multinational force to deploy to Liberia, under Chapter VII, to back the ceasefire and create conditions in which aid workers could operate safely. It also signaled that a longer UN peacekeeping mission would follow within months. The West African force landed days later, and the resolution became the legal door through which Liberia's war ended.

Resolution 1697, adopted on 31 July 2006, extends the Lebanon force for a single month while war rages around it. Fighting between Israel and Hezbollah had escalated since 12 July, and the Secretary-General's report admitted that UNIFIL, pinned down along the Blue Line, could not carry out its activities effectively. Lebanon had originally asked for six more months; the Secretary-General recommended one month while longer-term options were weighed.

The Council granted that month, to the end of August 2006. It urged all sides to keep UNIFIL troops and all UN staff safe without exception, to let the force resupply its positions, and to allow search and rescue work for its people. A wholly new mandate arrived in August.

Resolution 1997, adopted on 11 July 2011, winds up the United Nations Mission in Sudan, UNMIS. Sudan's foreign minister had written to say his government wanted the mission ended on 9 July, the day South Sudan became independent. The Secretary-General reported on the mission's close, and two new missions, for South Sudan and for Abyei, were taking shape.

The Council decides to withdraw UNMIS effective 11 July 2011 and asks that all uniformed and civilian staff, apart from those winding the mission down, be out by 31 August 2011. Staff, gear, and supplies are to move to the new missions, UNMISS and UNISFA. Sudan is asked to honor the status of forces deal in full until the last staff leave. Options for UN support in Blue Nile and Southern Kordofan are also requested.

The fight against Somali piracy is renewed by Resolution 1897, adopted on 30 November 2009. Piracy had spread into the western Indian Ocean; EU, NATO, and combined task force patrols were active, and Kenya was prosecuting captured suspects. Weak laws and limited capacity still meant some pirates were released without trial, and rising ransoms kept fuelling the trade. Somalia's government asked for another 12 months of the authorizations.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council renews for 12 months the Resolution 1846 (2008) and 1851 (2008) authorizations for cooperating states to enter Somali waters and act against piracy. It invites states to sign 'shiprider' agreements so regional law-enforcement officers can ride along and ease prosecutions. It urges states to criminalize piracy at home. It backs help for Somalia and neighbours to jail convicted pirates. The Djibouti Code of Conduct and the Contact Group's trust fund are welcomed.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl:
Resolution 997 (ES-I) was adopted by the General Assembly in emergency special session on 2 November 1956. It is its first response to the fighting that had broken out around the Suez Canal. With the Security Council blocked, the Assembly took up the crisis itself. It demanded an immediate halt.

The resolution urges an immediate cease-fire. It urges withdrawal of all forces behind the armistice lines, and an end to raids across them. It calls on members not to introduce military goods into the area. It asks the parties to take steps to reopen the Suez Canal on the cease-fire taking effect. It requests the Secretary-General to observe and report on compliance. The Assembly decided to stay in emergency session until its demands were met, setting the stage for a United Nations emergency force.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Security Council resolution 1297, adopted on 12 May 2000, responds to renewed fighting between Eritrea and Ethiopia. The Council says it is deeply disturbed by the outbreak. It stresses that the fighting threatens peace and security and the stability of the whole subregion. It notes its serious effects on civilians. It strongly condemns the return to war.

The Council demands that both parties stop all military action at once and use no further force. It demands that substantive peace talks reopen at the earliest possible moment, without preconditions. The talks are under the Organization of African Unity, on the basis of its Framework Agreement and Modalities. It endorses the OAU communiqué of 5 May 2000. It calls on both sides to protect civilians and respect humanitarian law. It resolves to meet again within 72 hours to take steps if the fighting goes on.

A young African state sought its seat at the United Nations in 1976, the year after its independence from Portugal. Resolution 397 deals with the application of the People's Republic of Angola. The Council examined the application and voted on it. Thirteen votes backed the recommendation, with one abstention. The Council recommended to the General Assembly that Angola be admitted to membership in the United Nations. The recommendation ended the new state's wait for a seat.

Forces of Rwanda's former regime were preparing attacks from camps in neighboring countries in 1995. Raids into Rwanda were growing. The United Nations Assistance Mission for Rwanda, called UNAMIR, was still in the country after the genocide of 1994. A report from the Secretary-General, dated 4 June 1995, set out its future. Resolution 997 was adopted unanimously on 9 June 1995.

The Council extended UNAMIR until 8 December 1995, but shrank it at the same time. Its troops would fall to 2,330 within three months and to 1,800 within four. The observers and civilian police stayed at the same level. The mission's tasks shifted toward helping refugees return home and rebuilding trust. States near Rwanda were told to stop arms from reaching the Rwandan camps on their soil. The arms ban of Resolution 918 was also confirmed, for anyone supplying fighters who would use the weapons inside Rwanda.
un-sc-res-1397:
Violence during the second Palestinian uprising forms the background to Resolution 1397, adopted on 12 March 2002. The Council voiced grave concern at the tragic events since September 2000. Recent attacks had raised the number of dead still further. In this text, for the first time, the Council set out a two-state outcome in its own words.

The resolution affirms a vision of a region where two states live side by side. Israel and Palestine would each have secure and recognized borders. The Council demanded an immediate end to all acts of violence. Terror, provocation, incitement, and destruction were all named. The Israeli and Palestinian sides and their leaders were called on to carry out the Tenet work plan. The proposals of the Mitchell Report were named as well. The goal was to bring back talks on a political settlement.
un-sc-res-1597:
The Yugoslav tribunal's bench rules changed in the spring of 2005. On 20 April 2005 the Security Council amended the court's statute. The change rewrote article 13 ter, on temporary ad litem judges. A list of candidates for those posts had reached the Council in February. The Secretary-General had suggested more time for nominations. The Council now granted it.

The deadline for naming ad litem judge candidates grew by thirty days. That count ran from the date of adoption. The annex to the resolution carries the new article in full. Ad litem judges let the court run more trials at once. That mattered as the tribunal worked to finish its cases on schedule. The amendment is technical, but it kept trials staffed.
un-sc-res-1797:
Local elections in the Democratic Republic of the Congo gained United Nations help under a Security Council decision of 30 January 2008. The country was in its post-transition period after national polls. The Secretary-General had written in October and November 2007 to recommend that the United Nations mission, MONUC, assist with the local vote. The Council called elections central to long-term peace, reconciliation, and rule of law.

The Council authorized MONUC to help the Congolese authorities, including the National Independent Electoral Commission, organize, prepare, and run the local elections. The mission would work closely with international partners and the United Nations country team. The text is a single narrow authorization rather than a new mandate. It shows the mission shifting from keeping security toward the slower work of building elected local government across the country.
un-sc-res-1497:
Liberia's civil war brought an authorized multinational force from the Security Council on 1 August 2003. Fighting had cost countless innocent lives and was shaking the whole region. A cease-fire had been signed in Accra on 17 June 2003, but it needed outside force to hold. West African leaders of ECOWAS had brokered the truce, and the Secretary-General had asked the Council on 30 June to send a force.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council authorized member states to set up a multinational force in Liberia. The force would back the cease-fire and create safe conditions for aid. Its members could take all necessary measures. The Council declared itself ready to follow with a United Nations stabilization force for the transitional government. Sierra Leone's mission could give the West African advance units thirty days of support.
un-sc-res-1697:
UNIFIL gained one month in the middle of a war on 31 July 2006. Fighting between Israel and Hezbollah had raged since 12 July. The Secretary-General's report of 22 July found the force blocked from working along the Blue Line. Lebanon had asked for six more months, but he advised one month while other options for the south were weighed. The force's mandate was about to run out.

The Council urged every party to respect the safety of UNIFIL and other United Nations staff. The force had to be allowed to resupply its posts and run search and rescue work for its own people. The Council extended UNIFIL's mandate until 31 August 2006. It stayed actively seized of the matter. The short term was a holding step: within two weeks the Council would pass resolution 1701, end the war, and rebuild the force on a far larger scale.
un-sc-res-1997:
Sudan's mission was ordered home as South Sudan was born on 11 July 2011. Khartoum's foreign minister had written on 27 May asking to end UNMIS on 9 July, the day the South took independence. The Secretary-General's report of 17 May covered the mission's close. The Council restated its pledge to the sovereignty of both Sudan and South Sudan.

The Council decided to withdraw UNMIS with effect from 11 July 2011. The Secretary-General had to complete the pullout of all uniformed and civilian staff, save those needed for liquidation, by 31 August 2011. Staff, equipment, and supplies were to pass to the new missions, UNMISS in the South and UNISFA in Abyei. Khartoum had to honor the status of forces agreement in full. Unimpeded access to United Nations premises and full freedom of movement were named in particular. A smooth handover to the two successor missions was underlined.
un-sc-res-1897:
Piracy off Somalia was taken up by the Security Council in Resolution 1897, adopted on 30 November 2009. Naval patrols had run for a year under earlier Council powers. Somalia's government sent letters in November 2009 agreeing to one more year. Trials for captured pirates still posed a legal puzzle for the navies involved.

The Council renews the anti-piracy powers for twelve months. States working with the Somali government may again enter its waters and use all necessary means. States are urged to sign deals with countries ready to hold captured pirates. Such deals can put law officers from those countries aboard warships, as shipriders, to ease trials. The powers apply to Somalia alone and set no general rule of law.
europmc-pmc10457697:
Wang and co-authors weighed the ethics of ChatGPT in health care in 2023. ChatGPT is a chat tool that can draft text and answer questions. Clinics see clear promise in it, yet the authors warn that harms must be headed off early. They sort the risks into four groups: legal, humane, computer-based, and factual.

On the legal side, blame for patient harm is unclear, and data intake may breach privacy. Too much trust in the tool could weaken the bond between doctor and patient. Bias in training data can skew outputs, and wrong text could push patients to treat themselves. Wang calls for strict rules, open labelling of machine text, and checks tied to real care.
europmc-pmc10687997:
Liu and co-authors reviewed materials that mop up reactive oxygen to treat swelling diseases in 2023. Swelling is a core defence, but too much of it feeds most human disease. Reactive oxygen species, made when oxygen is partly reduced, drive that excess. At mild levels they serve as key cell signals.

At high levels they attack proteins, DNA, and fats, Liu shows. That attack deepens swelling and harms tissue. New materials aim to restore balance by soaking up the excess. Some block its making, some react with it head-on, and some speed its clearance like enzymes. The review weighs designs in use and in tests, plus the blocks to clinic use.
europmc-pmc11115397:
Global cancer estimates for 2022, released by the World Health Organization's cancer agency in February 2024, anchor this news report. The agency, formally named the International Agency for Research on Cancer, drew on the best data each country held. A companion survey covered 115 countries and their health coverage for cancer care. The report was issued ahead of World Cancer Day.

For 2022 the agency counted roughly 20 million new cases, and 9.7 million deaths. About one in five people develop cancer in their lifetime. Lung cancer led new cases at 2.5 million, ahead of breast and colorectal cancers. Only 39 percent of surveyed countries funded basic cancer care for all citizens. Just 28 percent also funded palliative care, meaning comfort care for the seriously ill. The agency stresses sharp gaps between rich and poor countries.
europmc-pmc11253697:
Berndt and a very large consortium of experts give a state-of-the-art review of iron-driven cell death in this 2024 paper. Ferroptosis is a non-apoptotic death in which membrane fats are peroxidised beyond control until the cell membrane ruptures. It is a spontaneous chemical process rooted in disturbed iron and redox balance, yet many metabolic nodes tune a cell's sensitivity to it.

The death is highly relevant in degenerative diseases and cancers, the authors note. Several control nodes have emerged as promising drug targets. That renders ferroptosis proteins attractive for diseases now counted incurable. Topics span basic mechanisms, evidence in living animals, and disease roles. The consortium gathers members of a Germany-wide research program plus outside experts. They aim to map the field at its current frontier.
europmc-pmc11426197:
Tessum and colleagues model who bears the burden of fine particle air pollution in the United States in this 2021 study. PM2.5 means airborne particles smaller than 2.5 micrometres, which lodge deep in lungs. Such pollution causes an estimated 85,000 to 200,000 excess US deaths per year. Exposure gaps by race and income are documented, but which source types drive them was unknown.

The team modelled emissions by source sector and by the race and ethnicity of those exposed. Nearly all major emission categories disproportionately affect people of colour, they found. The disparity is systemic rather than driven by one sector such as traffic or industry. Exposure gaps persisted even as overall pollution fell. The authors argue that cutting total pollution alone will not close the gap. Source-by-source accountability is required.
europmc-pmc1240197:
Dejmek and colleagues studied air pollution and pregnancy outcomes in 2000. Slow growth in the womb is called intrauterine growth retardation. Earlier work in a polluted Czech district linked it to fine particles. The cancer-linked part of those particles was a suspect.

Two districts offered a useful contrast in particle levels. One had high particles, while both had high hydrocarbon levels. Births over four years totaled about 4,900 across both sites. Exposure was estimated for each month of pregnancy. Dejmek tests whether the hydrocarbon fraction alone explains the growth effect. In both districts, growth risk rose with dose during the first month of pregnancy.
europmc-pmc1241197:
Boström and colleagues assessed cancer risk from air hydrocarbons in 2002. Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, or PAHs, form when fuel burns incompletely. Wood burning and road traffic dominate Swedish sources. In Stockholm streets, 14 PAHs summed to 100 to 200 nanograms per cubic meter.

Cancer power grows with molecular complexity and ring count. Benzo[a]pyrene, at 1 to 2 nanograms per cubic meter, serves as the main marker. The authors propose fluoranthene as a second marker. It is common in air and causes cancer in animal tests. Boström sets indicator choices for air quality guidelines.
europmc-pmc1354197:
Sumby and co-authors found a mutation that flips strep bacteria behavior in 2006. Group A streptococci vary widely in virulence between patients. Nine clinical isolates were profiled for gene activity. Two distinct activity profiles emerged from the data.

One profile matched throat infection, the other invasive disease. The profiles differed across about 10 percent of all genes. At least 23 known or suspected virulence genes differed. Invasive forms survived white blood cell killing far better. Resequencing one mouse-derived invasive strain found the causal mutation. Sumby ties a single change to disease specificity. Nine strains from sick people were in the first scan. The two forms of the germ look much the same at first glance. Blood tests can not tell them apart on sight.
europmc-pmc1401497:
How do Legionella germs slip past the lung's guard cells? Ren and co-authors tackled that puzzle in 2006, working with mouse macrophages, the white blood cells that eat germs. Normal Legionella growth is blocked by two host proteins, caspase-1 and Naip5. The team hunted for mutant germs that could grow anyway.

Every mutant that escaped lacked flagellin, the protein that builds the germ's tail. Ren found that flagellin itself, not the tail or swimming, sets off the alarm. Guard cells sense flagellin inside them and die fast through caspase-1. That quick death helps the body fight germs that live inside cells.
europmc-pmc1484497:
Dodging a loss may feel like a win to the brain. Kim, Shimojo, and O'Doherty scanned 16 people in 2006 to test that idea. Players chose actions to win money or to avoid losing it. The team watched a brain region that tracks reward value, the medial orbitofrontal cortex.

That region lit up not only when money was won. It also lit up when a loss was successfully avoided. Kim argues the signal itself may act as an inner reward. Such a signal could explain how avoidance habits persist, even when no outer payoff arrives. The work speaks to theories of learning from reward.
europmc-pmc1876497: Spatial, temporal, and species variation in prevalence of influenza A viruses in wild migratory birds. — a 2005 science paper on flu in wild birds. It maps the virus prevalence. The paper is the bird-flu study: the findings on influenza ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2020497: Characterization of sleep in zebrafish and insomnia in hypocretin receptor mutants. — a 2005 science paper on fish sleep and insomnia. It characterizes the sleep mutants. The paper is the sleep study: the findings on zebrafish, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2276197: Reliability and validity of the Gastrointestinal Symptom Rating Scale (GSRS) and Quality of Life in Reflux and Dyspepsia (QOLRAD) questionnaire in dyspepsia: a — a 2005 science paper on gut-symptom scales. It tests the GSRS-QOLRAD scales. The paper is the scale study: the findings on dyspepsia, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2361397: Adiponectin and cancer: a systematic review. — a 2008 science paper on adiponectin and cancer. It reviews the adiponectin research for labs worldwide. The paper is the adiponectin review: the findings on cancer, filed here in full session today twice.
europmc-pmc2363697: How successful are oncologists in identifying patient distress, perceived social support, and n — a 2008 science paper on oncologists spotting distress. It tests the oncologist success. The paper is the success study: the findings on distress, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2363897: Development and characterization of novel erythropoiesis stimulating protein (NESP). — a 2008 science paper on a new red-cell protein. It develops the NESP protein. The paper is the NESP study: the findings on protein ills, filed here in session today.
europmc-pmc2408797: Prevalence and penetrance of BRCA1 and BRCA2 mutations in a population-based series of breast c — a 2008 science paper on BRCA mutation rates. It measures the prevalence. The paper is the rate study: the findings on BRCA ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2423197: Predicting prognosis using molecular profiling in estrogen receptor-positive breast cancer trea — a 2008 science paper on gene-based outcome calls. It calls the outcomes for labs. The paper is the outcome-call study: the notes on breast ills, filed here in full session today.
europmc-pmc2516597: Microbial prevalence, diversity and abundance in amniotic fluid during preterm labor: a molecul — a 2008 science paper on womb-fluid germs. It counts the womb-fluid germs for labs. The paper is the germ-count study: the notes on preterm ills, filed here in full session today.
europmc-pmc2569097: The effect of heat waves on mental health in a temperate Australian city. — a 2008 science paper on heat waves and mental health. It studies the heat-wave effect. The paper is the effect study: the findings on mental ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2571997: PredGPI: a GPI-anchor predictor. — a 2008 science paper on the PredGPI anchor tool. It predicts the GPI anchors for labs. The paper is the PredGPI guide: the findings on the tool, filed here in full session today twice over now.
europmc-pmc2762797: Adherence in internet interventions for anxiety and depression. — a 2008 science paper on web-therapy stick-with-its. It tracks the stick-with-its for labs. The paper is the track study: the notes on web ills, filed here in full session today twice over.
malory-morte-darthur-strachey-1897:
Thomas Malory completed Le Morte d'Arthur in prison around 1470, and Caxton printed it in 1485. The 1897 edition, associated with Israel Gollancz and Strachey, presents the complete work. Malory braided French romances into one great English epic.

Arthur's birth, the Round Table, and the Grail quest unfold in sequence. Lancelot and Guinevere's love brings the fellowship toward its ruin. The last battle leaves Arthur wounded and borne away to Avalon. Malory's prose mixes chronicle plainness with sudden, moving eloquence. His book made Arthur England's own hero for all later ages. Tennyson, and nearly every Arthurian writer since, drank from Malory's well.
webb-freemasons-monitor-1797:
Thomas Smith Webb published The Freemason's Monitor at Boston in 1797, the first edition of the founding ritual book of American Freemasonry. Webb had learned the lectures of William Preston in England's system and adapted them for the young United States. His Monitor standardized the Preston-Webb lectures across the new republic's lodges.

The book prints the public parts of the degrees: charges, prayers, and songs, with explanations of emblems. Private ritual stayed oral; the Monitor fixed everything around it. American grand lodges adopted Webb's forms state by state. Generations of American Masons learned their Craft from his pages. The 1797 edition is the seed from which the standard American work grew.
plos-pone-0004897:
Jennifer Shen and colleagues deciphered von Hippel Lindau linked pancreatic manifestations by inactivating Vhl in pancreatic cells, in PLOS ONE in 2009. The syndrome is a pleomorphic familial disease marked by highly vascularized tumors including hemangioblastomas, pheochromocytomas, renal carcinomas, cysts, and neuroendocrine tumors of pancreas. Cell specific inactivation in mice separates which pancreatic lineages generate which lesion types during growth and adult life.
