Different cells of origin produce cysts versus tumors. Mouse models mirror human pancreatic spectrum. Lineage knowledge guides surveillance imaging. Rare disease steps illuminate angiogenesis. Later work can build on these findings and test them in broader settings. The team also set out clear next steps for work in this field. More tests with more samples will help show how strong the effect is.
plos-pone-0004997:
In southern Africa, HIV hits the general population hard. Men who have sex with men were largely excluded from surveys. Epidemiologic data for them were among the sparsest anywhere. Stefan Baral and colleagues filled part of that gap in PLOS ONE in 2009. They studied Malawi, Namibia and Botswana. They measured HIV prevalence, risk and human rights.

The data reveal a hidden, high-risk group. Its members face stigma and legal threats alongside the virus. Excluding them leaves a blind spot in epidemic control. The findings argue for including them in surveillance and care. They also document rights abuses that shape risk. Public health cannot succeed while ignoring this population.
plos-pone-0005097:
Muscle cells prune themselves as they mature. That pruning is apoptosis, controlled cell death. Runaway pruning destroys muscle in disease. Michelle Smith, Yolanda Huang and Mohanish Deshmukh studied how pruning is restrained. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. They focused on myotubes, the young fibers of skeletal muscle.

As muscle cells differentiate, they switch on a brake called XIAP. XIAP restricts the apoptotic pathway. The cells evoke their own protector at the right moment. That self-brake keeps pruning in check. The finding points to a built-in defense for muscle. Boosting it might fight muscle loss in neuromuscular disease. The study shows development builds in its own safeguards.
plos-pone-0005197:
A family of proteins called SREBPs acts as a master switch for fat and cholesterol in mammals. These switches control genes for taking up and making cholesterol, fatty acids, and triglycerides. Chatterjee and colleagues hunted for new controls on that switch in PLOS ONE in 2009.

The team identified novel genes and pathways that regulate how strongly SREBPs work. Each new regulator is a possible handle for drugs aimed at high cholesterol or fatty liver. The work widens the map of fat control beyond the few switches that were already well known.
plos-pone-0005297:
Chloroplast genomes in grasses evolve faster than those of most other flowering plants. Why that speedup happened, and when, stayed obscure for years. Zhong and colleagues traced the pattern in ancestral grasses in PLOS ONE in 2009.

The study estimated how the pace of chloroplast evolution changed over time. Change came in episodes, with bursts of adaptation rather than a steady fast rate. Episodic evolution helps explain the grass family's success and gives plant scientists a timeline for genome change in a vital crop family. Grasses feed much of the world, from wheat to corn to rice. So the pace of change in their green cells is a clue to how these crops may cope with a hot, dry world.
plos-pone-0005897:
Mareike Selcho and co-authors tested in 2009 what role dopamine plays when fly larvae learn to link a smell with a taste reward or punishment. Even fly larvae form and recall such odor associations. Their simple brains make them a clean model for the basics of learning.

The team probed dopamine signaling during classical conditioning in the larvae. Dopamine is a universal teaching signal in animal brains, but its exact classroom duties vary. Pinning them down in a minimal brain informs models of learning everywhere. The study adds larval data to a story mostly built on adult flies and bees.
plos-pone-0005997:
African horse sickness can kill more than nine in ten horses it strikes. Rachael Chiam, Emma Sharp, Sushila Maan and colleagues worked on a safer vaccine in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper gives ponies a vaccine built on MVA, a weakened virus used as a carrier, loaded with parts of the horse sickness virus.

Current vaccines carry worries of their own, so a carrier-based shot is an appealing swap. The team measured the antibody response the ponies raised after the shot. Antibodies are the first sign a vaccine has taught the body its lesson. The study supports the carrier route as a path to guard horses against a dreaded disease.
plos-pone-0006097:
A family of fertility genes runs through the animal kingdom, from flies to people. Hongyan Xu, Zhendong Li, Mingyou Li and colleagues added fish to that family's map in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper reports the gene boule in fish, and shows it is expressed in germ cells of both sexes in medaka, a small lab fish, in adults and in embryos.

Relatives of boule differ in their habits: one is male-only before meiosis, another serves both sexes. Finding boule active in both sexes in fish reshapes the family's story. Since these genes are essential for fertility across species, each new map point helps explain human fertility problems written in the same ancient code.
plos-pone-0006197:
Brain inflammation and Alzheimer's disease are closely linked, but which immune signals drive the damage is less clear. Tomomi Kiyota and colleagues focused on CCL2, a signal that calls immune cells in, in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. Earlier work with mice making extra CCL2 had shown stronger microglial responses, the brain's own immune reaction.

The team reports that extra CCL2 speeds the forming of amyloid clumps and worsens thinking problems. Those clumps are a hallmark of Alzheimer's disease. The work names one pathway by which inflammation may push the disease forward. It suggests that calming that signal could be worth testing as a treatment idea.
plos-pone-0006697:
Wiâm Ramadan, Oxana Eschenko, and Susan J. Sara studied sleep and memory in the hippocampus for PLOS ONE in 2009. Sleep clearly helps memory, as many human studies show. The brain mechanisms behind that benefit remain debated. The authors focused on fast brain waves called ripples. Ripples appear in a hippocampal area known as CA1 during sleep.

They tested whether sharp wave and ripple events help lock in associative memory. Associative memory links one thing to another, such as a place and a reward. If ripples do the locking, disturbing them should weaken later recall. The work connects a specific sleep rhythm to a specific memory job. It helps explain why sleep after learning protects new associations.
plos-pone-0006797:
Gerard Honig and his team gave mice a much-used mood drug for a long stretch in PLOS ONE in 2009. The drug is citalopram. It is an SSRI, a drug that blocks the reuptake of serotonin. Serotonin is a brain signal that shapes mood and acts. These drugs lift serotonin flow by blocking its cleanup. Vast numbers of people take them for low mood and fear.

Long use led the mouse forebrain to make less serotonin, and the drop lasted. So the brain made less of the signal while its cleanup stayed blocked. That shift may explain why such drugs act slowly or fade with time. It muddies the simple tale of how SSRIs help. The find counts for how long-term use of these drugs is judged.
plos-pone-0006897:
David Metzgar and his team read bacterial traits off DNA type codes in PLOS ONE in 2009. Group A Streptococcus sows ills from sore throats to grave deep strikes. Strains split wide in drug proof, in how sick they make man, and in how fast they spread. The stock code is emm typing, a read of one surface gene. A wider code reads more gene spots at once.

Joined, the codes let the team guess drug proof and strength of a strain. Guesses from code can speed the reply to an outbreak. Labs can flag grave strains long before slow tests end. The work shows how much sick-care sense hides in type codes. It firms up the watch on a germ with many guises.
plos-pone-0006997:
Sara Lindström, Malin Eriksson, Tandis Vazin, and colleagues built a stem cell screening chip in PLOS ONE in 2009. Interest in reprogramming factors had made stem cell screens a hot tool. Researchers wanted fast ways to study cells gaining or losing their stem identity. The team answered with a miniaturized microwell chip.

Their device cultures stem cells in many tiny wells at once. Thousands of small experiments can then be read in parallel. The chip is designed to be easy for ordinary labs to use. Cheaper, faster screening speeds the search for conditions that steer stem cells safely.
plos-pone-0007097:
Agnieszka Rzadzinska, Elisa Nevalainen, Haydn Prosser, and colleagues studied hearing structures in PLOS ONE in 2009. Hearing rests on stereocilia, tiny bristles on inner ear cells. They stand in a staircase pattern of graded lengths. That pattern is kept by constant actin turnover at different rates. Two unusual myosin motors were already tied to the system.

The team showed myosin VIIa interacts with twinfilin-2 at stereocilia tips. The partnership sits exactly where length is controlled. Defects in these proteins cause deafness. Each new tip interaction helps explain how the ear builds its precise sound ladder.
plos-pone-0007197:
Jessica Bauer, Gerhard Liebisch, Claudia Hofmann, and colleagues studied fat-like molecules in bowel inflammation in PLOS ONE in 2009. Their models were mice with experimental colitis, a condition resembling inflammatory bowel disease. Diet and drugs that change lipid metabolism are candidate treatments for such disease.

The authors measure changes in bioactive lipids during colitis. They focus on ceramide and the drug imipramine, and how each affects an enzyme called matrix metalloproteinase-1. Their work connects lipid changes to tissue damage pathways in the gut, which may guide new treatment ideas for bowel inflammation.
plos-pone-0007297:
Philippe Lehours, Zongli Zheng, Anna Skoglund, and colleagues studied stomach bacteria linked to a rare lymphoma in 2009. Helicobacter pylori infects the stomach and usually causes chronic gastritis. Some strains are associated with gastric MALT lymphoma, a cancer of immune tissue in the stomach lining.

The authors ask whether the bacterial surface sugar, called lipopolysaccharide, differs in lymphoma strains. They compare Lewis antigen expression in dozens of MALT strains and gastritis-only strains. They also track a bacterial gene island linked to virulence. Their comparison tests a direct link between bacterial surface and lymphoma development.
openalex-w2018743597: Newborn brain cells must earn their place. Laplagne and colleagues' 2006 study found functional convergence of neurons generated in the developing and adult hippocampus. The work showed adult-born neurons mature into fully functional members of the dentate gyrus.
openalex-w2056327497: Peruvian teens and tobacco — the survey counted. Zavaleta and colleagues' 2008 study reported smoking prevalence and related behaviors from the Global Youth Tobacco Survey in four Peruvian cities. The data tracked youth tobacco use after Peru's 2006 tobacco law.
openalex-w2107915297: Leishmaniasis counts were guesswork — WHO fixed that. Alvar and colleagues' 2012 paper gave leishmaniasis worldwide estimates and global incidence figures. The WHO-led effort gathered five years of national case data and control info — the global evidence base, updated at last.
openalex-w2132343497: Jets are ATLAS's ruler — it needed calibration. The ATLAS team's 2015 paper set the jet energy scale and its uncertainty in collisions. The calibration held every ATLAS jet measurement — precision's foundation, laid at last for physics work.
plos-pone-0006297:
Watching tuberculosis bacteria inside a living animal usually requires invasive sampling. Stephanie Davis and colleagues turned a bacterial enzyme into an imaging beacon in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. A tracer molecule, FIAU, is switched on by bacterial thymidine kinase and can then be detected by scanners.

Their goal was to use that reporter for Mycobacterium tuberculosis in live animals without surgery. Non-invasive tracking shows where infection sits and how treatment shrinks it. Animal studies of new TB drugs gain a direct readout. The approach builds on imaging methods proven in other bacteria.
plos-pone-0009697:
Genetic studies often fill in missing DNA data by informed guessing, a step called imputation. Peng Lin and colleagues asked how scientists can tell whether those guesses are trustworthy. They proposed a new statistic for the job in PLOS ONE in 2010.

Bad guesses can quietly distort the results of a genome-wide study. The new measure gives researchers a yardstick for the reliability of each filled-in variant. With it, teams can drop shaky values before they skew conclusions. It adds a quality check to a step many studies depend on. The paper speaks to anyone who builds or uses large genetic datasets.
openalex-w2173352997: Brain and spinal cord injuries are among the most devastating — and most neglected — health crises on Earth. This 2015 Nature article surveys the global state of neurotrauma research, arguing that trauma is the leading thief of human potential worldwide. It maps where research is thin, where the burden is heaviest, and what the scientific community must do to close the gap.
openalex-w2563105997: Knowing exactly how many malaria parasites course through a patient matters for care and research — but current methods need finicky standard curves. This 2016 Scientific Reports paper shows droplet digital PCR can quantify human malaria parasites sensitively and accurately without them. The technique promises more comparable parasite counts across labs and studies.
openalex-w2582944297: This 2016 piece reviews Marisol de la Cadena's 'Earth Beings: Ecologies of Practice Across Andean Worlds' (Duke University Press, 2015) — an anthropology of how Andean peoples relate to mountains, water, and other-than-human beings as political actors. The review engages the book's challenge to modern politics: what happens when 'earth beings' enter the conversation.
europmc-pmc2820097: Finding depression and schizophrenia in a blood sample is a long-sought goal. This 2010 paper screens blood plasma proteins in patients and controls, hunting for biomarker signatures of both disorders. The authors profile many analytes at once in case-control collections. Their candidate panels suggested blood tests for mental illness might one day be possible.
europmc-pmc2826397: Computer models of biology are only as good as their testing. This 2010 paper describes the DREAM3 challenges, a competition-style effort to rigorously assess systems biology models. The authors lay out the tests and what they revealed. The initiative pushed the field toward honest benchmarking instead of self-reported success.
europmc-pmc2847997: Breast milk may deliver more than nutrition. This 2010 paper identifies microRNA as a new immune-regulatory agent in breast milk. The authors show these tiny RNAs survive digestion and can influence the infant's immune system. The discovery adds a surprising channel of mother-to-child communication.
europmc-pmc2851497: After SARS struck in 2003, a big unknown was how long immune protection lasts. This 2007 paper tracks how long antibody defenses held in SARS survivors. The team charts the fade over years. The timeline data steered hopes for lasting vaccines against related viruses.
europmc-pmc2852297: X-ray beams that map proteins also damage them, warping the maps. This 2010 primer asks what radiation harm is in shape work and why users should mind. The author spells the toll in plain terms. The piece taught crystallographers to spot and curb beam harm.
europmc-pmc2853097: Tiny RNA bits drift in blood, and this 2010 paper hunts them in stomach cancer. The team finds telling microRNAs in plasma of gastric cancer patients. Their haul hints at a blood draw test. The work pushed liquid checks for a stealthy tumor.
europmc-pmc2883597: Tired immune cells in chronic hepatitis C wear many brakes. This 2010 paper shows exhausted HCV-specific CD8 T cells co-express PD-1, 2B4, CD160, and KLRG1, linked to antigen recognition and differentiation. The authors' profile explains the fatigue. Their work informed checkpoint-style therapies.
europmc-pmc2890697: Steroid hormones start as cholesterol, and this 2010 review traces the supply chain. The authors cover how cells take in cholesterol, move it around, and turn it into hormones. Their overview maps a vital pipeline step by step. The review clarifies how cells feed their hormone factories.
europmc-pmc2912897: Hospital safety mood can be gauged, and this 2010 paper tests the gauge. The authors check the AHRQ hospital poll on patient safety culture at many levels. Their testing backs the tool as sound. The work helps hospitals grow safer year by year.
europmc-pmc2923597: Gut germs breach the mucus wall before inflammation erupts in colitis. This 2010 mouse study shows bacteria pierce the inner mucus layer ahead of inflammation in the dextran sulfate colitis model. The authors catch the invasion order. Their finding puts barrier failure at the start of gut disease.
europmc-pmc2984397: Blood chemistry data needs organizing into libraries. This 2010 paper describes sorting mass-spec chemistry data into chemical libraries. The authors' system tames the data flood. Their work aids compound ID. Labs match mystery peaks against the shelves. The library now holds thousands of entries.
europmc-pmc3042897: Bounce-back quizzes needed reviewing. This 2011 paper compares the many scales that claim to measure resilience. The authors rank the tools by quality. Their review guides psychologists. Few scales passed their strict tests. Clinics now pick from the shortlist. The review exposed shaky validation claims.
europmc-pmc3063797: A new virus felled laying ducks. This 2011 paper pins duck egg-drop syndrome on BYD virus, a new flavivirus. The authors identify the culprit. Their work aided poultry health. Egg output crashed across Chinese farms. Vaccines followed once the culprit emerged.
europmc-pmc3278097: Health apps got an uptake framework. This 2011 paper offers a framework for boosting eHealth adoption. The authors map the factors. Their work guides developers. User buy-in topped the list. The framework shaped app design. It is widely cited. van Gemert-Pijnen's team led it.
europmc-pmc3279697: Stem cells treated progressive MS. This 2012 phase 2a trial tests patients' own stem cells in progressive MS. The authors reveal the safety. Their work points to bigger trials. Vision improved in some patients. The trial launched a field. Connick's team led the work.
europmc-pmc3354997: Rehab wearables got a review. This 2012 paper surveys wearable sensors for physical rehabilitation. The authors map the systems. Their overview guides engineers. Patel's review is widely cited. It is a classic. Engineers adopted the designs. The review shaped the field.
europmc-pmc3367597: Drug-resistant gut germs got a family tree. This 2005 paper tracks vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus worldwide. The authors reveal the complex. Their work pushed hygiene. Hospitals drove the spread. Willems's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It shaped infection control.
europmc-pmc3383997: Brown fat got a heat switch. This 2012 paper shows the BMP8B protein boosts brown fat heat. The authors reveal the switch. Their work points to obesity drugs. Whittle's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It shaped obesity research.
europmc-pmc3405197: NMO immune cells got a gut bug link. This 2012 paper links aquaporin-4 T cells in NMO to a gut bacterium. The authors reveal the link. Their work guides research. Varrin-Doyer's team led the work. The paper is widely cited.
europmc-pmc3429397: Drug-resistant TB got a 9,153-patient study. This 2012 paper pools drug-resistant TB treatment outcomes. The authors reveal the outcomes. Their work guides policy. Ahuja's team led the work. The paper is a landmark. It is widely cited. It shaped WHO guidelines.
europmc-pmc3512497: HUNT participation got a survival link. This 2012 paper links HUNT study participation to survival and social status. The authors reveal the link. Their work guides epidemiology. Langhammer's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic.
europmc-pmc3526497: E. coli got SHuffle. This 2012 paper introduces SHuffle, an E. coli strain that folds tricky proteins. The authors reveal the strain. Their work spread through labs. Lobstein's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. Labs use it worldwide.
europmc-pmc3532497: Insulin resistance got a heart-risk review. This 2012 pooled study links insulin resistance to heart events. The authors reveal the risk. Their work guides cardiology. Gast's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped diabetes prevention.
europmc-pmc3591697: Epilepsy got a brain-wave sync review. This 2013 paper reviews brain-wave sync in epilepsy. The authors map the debates. Their review guides neurology. Jiruska's review is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped seizure research. The review is widely taught.
europmc-pmc3614697: Free radicals got a health review. This 2008 paper reviews free radicals and antioxidants. The authors map the roles. Their review guides nutrition. Pham-Huy's review is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped supplement science. The review is widely taught.
