arxiv-2601-06897:
Viktoriia Borovik and co-authors posted a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint deals with elimination ideals of plücker ideals and algebras with straightening laws. It came out on arXiv in 2026 as a PAPERS preprint. It is well known that the Plücker ideal defining the Grassmannian is generated by quadratic Plücker relations.

These relations form a reverse lexicographic Gröbner basis and endow the Plücker algebra with the structure of an algebra with straightening laws (ASL). Readers in the field get a short, focused account of the problem and the steps the authors take.
arxiv-2601-07297:
Bo-Lun Huang and colleagues wrote a 2026 arXiv preprint. The work covers WISE/CatWISE constraints on dysonian Waste-Heat technosignatures in nearby galaxies facilities. ArXiv posted the preprint in 2026 under its PAPERS collection. We search for galaxy-scale ( Dysonian ) waste heat in the mid-infrared using WISE .

Starting from the 2MASS Redshift Survey , we cross-match to CatWISE2020 and AllWISE , apply standard MIR AGN/starburst vetoes (Stern. Assef R90, Jarrett), and treat W1 and W2 as stellar baselines and W3 and W4 as constraining bands. The work gives specialists a compact account of the problem and one proposed way to handle it.
arxiv-2601-08097: Yongliang Miao, Yangyang Liang, and Mengnan Du present AdaJudge, a reward modeling method from Emory University. Their 2026 arXiv paper addresses a core step in aligning language models with human choices. Most reward models squeeze a full sequence into one score with a fixed pooling rule. The authors list two flaws in that habit. A fixed bias can miss task-dependent preference signals, and backbone features tuned for generation may suit fine judgment poorly. AdaJudge answers with adaptive judging from multiple perspectives.
arxiv-2601-08197: A natural account of galactic magnetic fields is offered through multistate scalar field dark matter. The 2026 arXiv paper, co-authored by Miguel Alcubierre, studies fields of order microgauss seen across galaxies. The authors test whether these fields arise from a complex scalar field dark matter halo. In their setup, the halo carries charge under a local U(1) symmetry. If the mechanism works, dark matter itself could seed the magnetic fields telescopes observe. That link would tie two open problems in astrophysics into one testable story.
arxiv-2601-08397: Shohei Aoki and co-authors build empirical transit spectra of Mars from TGO and NOMAD data. Their 2026 arXiv paper notes that transit spectroscopy probes exoplanet atmospheres, a powerful but tricky tool. Aerosols strongly affect spectra, and accounting for them is key to recovering atmospheric properties. Mars offers a well-characterized atmosphere to practice on. The team models its transit spectrum with petitRADTRANS and the Planetary Spectrum Generator. Lessons from Mars can sharpen how researchers read spectra of distant rocky planets.
arxiv-2601-08497: Jia-Xin He and Hung-Hsuan Chen present GraphFusionSBR for session-based recommendation. Their 2026 arXiv paper notes that session-based systems must infer user intent from short click sessions. Existing models suffer from item interaction dominance and noisy sessions. The authors propose a multi-channel model that denoises across three graph views. Channels include a knowledge graph, a session hypergraph, and a session line graph. Fusing several views aims to capture intent that any single graph would miss, improving suggestions for anonymous shoppers.
arxiv-2601-08597: Aryaman Patel and Dario Weissmann stratify moduli spaces of Higgs bundles through stability under covers. Their 2026 arXiv paper studies slope-stability of reflexive twisted sheaves over a normal projective variety. The question is how stability behaves under pullback along a cover. Stability is always preserved when the cover does not factor through a quasi-etale cover. One special cover checks stability across all Galois covers, yielding a stratification of the moduli space. The result organizes Higgs bundle moduli for algebraic geometers.
arxiv-2601-08697: Nifu Dan audits how online graduate computer science students collaborate with AI. The 2026 arXiv case study notes that generative AI now shapes how students complete academic tasks. These systems offer efficiency and support for learning and coding work. Concerns persist about over-automation, diminished student agency, and unreliable or hallucinated outputs. The audit examines real collaboration in one online graduate setting. Findings can help instructors set AI policies grounded in observed student behavior rather than guesswork.
arxiv-2604-01197:
Fangjun Hu and seven co-authors study learning mixed quantum states in 2026. Learning quantum states from measurement data is a central problem. It sits at the heart of quantum information and computational complexity.

They study learning to generate mixed states on a finite-dimensional lattice. Recent work on mixed state phases of matter motivates their focus. They concentrate on arbitrary states in the trivial phase specifically. Shallow channel circuits prepare the states they learn to reproduce. The question is how much data and computation generation requires. Their results speak to both physics and learning theory audiences. Readers get a careful case where quantum learning is tractable.
arxiv-2601-07497:
Sergio Conti and coauthors treat sharp edges in solids with smooth fields, in a 2026 analysis preprint. Their phase-field approach targets energies set on splits of a solid, built to model grain edges in polycrystals. Grains are small crystals with different orientations inside a metal or ceramic. The variable takes values in the orthogonal group, adjusted by the lattice point group.

That adjustment reflects the crystal symmetries of the underlying lattice. Two orientations that differ by a symmetry should count as the same physical state. A good approach must respect that match while still being fit for use in math work. Phase-field models see wide use to track how small scale forms grow. This work strengthens their mathematical base for polycrystals. Applied mathematicians and materials scientists both have reason to read it. The grains are tiny, yet their edges shape how strong or weak a solid is.
arxiv-2601-07697:
Anna Shapiro sets three formulas side by side for a new polynomial tied to polymatroids. The cave polynomial is new, and it was brought in to study syzygies of polymatroidal ideals. Syzygies describe relations among the equations defining an ideal. Her 2026 preprint studies the counting links between the three formulas. Each one counts the terms of the polynomial in its own way.

As a use, she reads the Snapper polynomial through all three of them. Multiple views of one object often reveal facts that a single view hides. Polymatroids generalize matroids, a core structure in combinatorics and optimization. The paper serves those who work in algebra and counting and who use such polynomials. It also shows how a new invariant can connect older, separate lines of work. Each view is short to state, yet each one brings out facts the rest can hide.
arxiv-2601-08997:
Ziqiang Guan and a large team study a nickel based stuff that splits into layers when it cools. The stuff is a three layer nickel oxide. In its wave state, charge piles in a set wave plan. The team reads that shift with slant light in the heat ray range. Light slant lets them split in plane from out of plane acts.

They find a sharp split. In plane, the stuff acts like a metal. Out of plane, it acts like a block. In the wave state, that split grows by more than ten fold. Out of plane flow all but stops. A reader in new stuffs gets a clear sign. Wave order can peel layers apart in how they carry charge.
arxiv-2601-09297:
Ioana-Claudia Lazar studies a class of shape groups built from triangle and pentagon tiles. Such groups act on spaces with a set bend rule, called CAT(0). That rule says triangles in the space are no fat than flat ones. It is a broad sign of a tame, no wild fold space. Tile groups of this kind are test cases for that tameness.

She shows a tile form of these groups has two neat local traits. It is 7-located and locally 5-large, in the terms of the field. Those traits give new cases of groups with both marks. A reader in group shape work gets fresh cases to test broad claims on.
arxiv-2601-09497:
Ritabrata Chakraborty and three co-authors probe why object detectors stumble on new datasets. Their 2026 arXiv paper studies cross-dataset object detection through the lens of setting specificity. A detector trained on one benchmark often scores far worse on another.

The authors sort benchmarks into two kinds: broad sets with varied everyday scenes, and narrow sets tied to one setting. They then run a standard detector family across all train-test pairs. The pattern of wins and losses shows how much of the drop comes from the setting itself. That diagnosis helps builders choose data that travels better.
arxiv-2601-09597:
Manish Chaudhary studies how to grow complex entanglement by letting a system leak in a controlled way. His 2026 arXiv paper treats dissipative state engineering with Markovian dynamics. Highly entangled states shared among many parties are key resources for quantum computing tasks.

The target here is a cluster-state pattern of entanglement in spins coupled by Ising interactions. Instead of shielding the system from its surroundings, the method engineers the leak itself. The engineered dissipation drives the spins toward the desired entangled state. Such recipes could make delicate states easier to prepare and hold.
arxiv-2601-09697:
Jieying Chen, Jeffrey Hu, Joan Lasenby, and Ayush Tewari make camera-controlled video generation fast enough to use. Their 2026 arXiv paper combines sparse diffusion with 3D rendering for static scenes. Diffusion video models make realistic clips but can need minutes of GPU time for seconds of footage.

That cost blocks real-time uses such as embodied AI and virtual or augmented reality. The authors shift work into a 3D render, using diffusion only where it is needed. Static scenes are the target, where geometry can carry most of the image. Faster generation opens interactive applications that current models cannot serve.
arxiv-2601-09897:
Nestor Colin and four co-authors extend a classic symmetry theorem to huge surfaces. Their 2026 arXiv paper proves a Birman-Hilden result for big mapping class groups. The surfaces involved are connected, without boundary, and either infinite in type or of negative Euler characteristic.

Given a fully ramified branched covering between two such surfaces, the authors prove it has the Birman-Hilden property. That property lifts symmetries of the base to the cover. Big mapping class groups govern infinite surfaces like flute surfaces. Work of this kind gives the field shared ground rules it did not have before. Extending the theorem there strengthens tools for a fast-growing area of study, one that more and more young researchers are now choosing to enter.
arxiv-2601-10197:
Maxwell West proves that some quantum states are hard to learn on mean. Two sets of states are in play. One set is drawn flat from all states. One set comes from free fermion states. A learner sees data from a state's birth spread.

West works in the stats query model. In that model, the learner asks for rough means, not raw data. He shows the task is hard on mean for both sets. Hard here means the query count must be vast. The work marks a bound on what such learners can do. It aids the map of quantum learn tasks.
arxiv-2601-10297:
Hans-Christoph Grunau and Marius Müller find whole space best forms for a fourth order free edge task. The task is a biharmonic form of the Alt Caffarelli model. Such models trade bulk cost against the size of a set where the field is live.

The team study forms that span all space. Half space forms win for the two sided case. They do not win in the one sided case. The team find a next class of best forms too. All forms in that class have a flat Laplacian. The work sorts which shapes can be global bests.
arxiv-2601-10397:
Genki Shimizu and Taro Toyoizumi build a theory of fast, linked change at nerve joins. A join can grow or shrink for a short span based on use. That fast change is named short term plasticity. It was seen as a pre side sieve for spikes. The post side was thought to play no role.

Fresh tests show the change can link both sides. It rests on pre and post fires at once. The team give a rule based theory for that link. Their theory rests on how much fact a join pass can carry. It shows why a linked form would aid a net.
arxiv-2601-10697:
Manuj Mukherjee, Sagnik Chatterjee, and Alhad Sethi study how parties can cook up a shared secret key from shared randomness. Nitinawarat and Narayan built a perfect scheme for the pairwise independent network model. That model's backbone is a graph, and the scheme leans on how many spanning trees the graph packs. The new work swaps the graph for a hypergraph.

In a hypergraph, one edge can join many parties at once. The authors push toward perfect key schemes that use the hypergraph's own structure. Perfect keys leak nothing to an eavesdropper. Extending the graph results would widen the networks where such strong secrecy is possible by design, not by extra hardware.
arxiv-2601-10797:
Alice Crafford and co-authors, with the LSST Dark Energy Science Collaboration, probe a weak point in photometric redshift work. Most science from the LSST survey will rest on photo-z estimates, distances inferred from galaxy colors. Training sets from spectroscopy anchor those estimates. If the training set is incomplete or skewed, bias creeps into every distance.

The authors diagnose how such training set flaws hurt photo-z performance. Knowing the failure modes lets survey teams correct or at least bound the bias. Distance bias would ripple into maps of dark matter and dark energy. This groundwork helps LSST keep its cosmology honest from the start.
arxiv-2601-10897:
Boris A. Malomed, Gennadiy Burlak, Gustavo Medina-Ángel, and Yuriy Karlovich study light from quantum nanoemitters set in a lattice of conducting nanorings. The emitters sit in a periodic array where plasmon polaritons, waves that mix light with electron motion, are excited. The team investigates the semiclassical dynamics of the optical field the emitters produce.

The focus falls on dynamical correlations and chimera-like states. In a chimera, some parts of a system move in sync while others drift apart. Seeing such states in a nano-optical lattice would link two lively fields. The results may guide devices that steer light at the nanoscale with patterns no uniform array could make.
arxiv-2601-11797:
Tenghao Li, Neha Sangwan, Xiaxin Li, and Arya Mazumdar study group testing when counts are noisy. In group testing, pools of samples are tested at once to find the few bad ones. The quantitative form asks how many bad ones sit in each pool.

They study three cases: no noise, added Gaussian noise, and a one-way noisy channel. For each case they test two methods. One scores links in a linear way, and one uses least squares fits. The work maps how well each method does as noise grows, which guides test design in labs.
arxiv-2601-12197:
Bihan Chatterjee, Siva Theja Maguluri, and Debankur Mukherjee refine the wait time spread in a classic queue. The M/G/1 queue has Poisson arrivals and general service times. In heavy traffic, the sojourn time tends to an exponential spread, a known limit.

They seek higher-order terms that hold before that limit. They use Stein's method to build those terms. Better finite-traffic forms help size real service systems. Call centres and cloud queues both need such pre-limit tools.  Stein terms add shape past the known limit form.  Pre limit forms are what real queues need, since no queue is at the limit.
arxiv-2601-11397:
Emma Hart, Bas Peters, Julianne Chung, and Matthias Chung infer hidden states with paired nets. Their 2026 preprint builds a latent space inference framework. Inverse problems ask what hidden cause made the seen data. Mismatches between observations can wreck classic solvers.

The frame uses two autoencoders trained as a pair. One net encodes the parameter space of the problem. The other encodes the observation space in matching form. Learned maps join the two latent spaces to each other. Inference then runs in the small latent world, not the raw one. That shift can absorb gaps between data sources. It offers a data-driven path to steadier inverse answers.
arxiv-2601-11497:
Yamato Fujii and five coauthors check a hidden error in reaction cross sections. Their 2026 preprint deals with alpha-particle activation measures. Below the Coulomb barrier, such reactions are faint and rare. Secondary neutrons in the setup can fake part of the signal.

The test reaction makes 195m Pt from natural platinum. Alpha hits drive it, but stray neutrons can drive it too. The team characterized the secondary neutron field first. They used the PHITS particle transport simulation code. Neutron-driven yields were then estimated from library data. The JENDL-5/A library gave the neutron cross sections used. Knowing the fake share keeps the true cross section honest.
arxiv-2601-11597:
Martin Rivas asks if one point can describe an electron in this preprint. His 2026 answer to the title question is yes. The point is not the whole electron in his view. It marks the location of the electron's center of charge.

Rivas reads the geometry of smooth curves in 3D space. That reading yields a system of differential equations. The system is of fourth order for the moving point. The point moves at the speed of light at all times. Such a picture gives the electron a sharp trajectory. It stands apart from the cloud views of standard theory. The claim invites fresh debate on what an electron is.
arxiv-2601-13097:
Elena Bruches and a large team present a small reward model for tests that need no run. Their tool scores unit tests that code models write on their own. Running each test can be slow, costly, or unsafe, so a run free score has clear worth.

The model is named RM-RF. It is kept light, so it can score many tests fast. A reward model of this kind can rank tests by how good they look. That rank can then steer a code model to write better tests. For teams that use AI to draft code, a fast test score helps pick which drafts to keep, run, or drop.
arxiv-2601-13497:
Jiayi Chen, Ming Lu, and Shiquan Ruan build a bridge of two rings, a Hall algebra and a ring of double symmetric functions. The Hall side comes from the Jordan quiver, the most plain quiver with one node and one loop. Its derived form counts how modules grow.

The next side holds symmetric sums in two sets of count less vars. Each set is held fixed by its own swaps, and a parameter t marks the ring. The team proves the two rings are the same in form. Such a bridge lets results proved on one side cross to the next. For algebra staff, a new bridge is a tool in its own right.
arxiv-2601-12597:
Ron M. Adin, Eli Bagno, and Yuval Roichman study how to turn one cyclic permutation into another. Their moves are conjugations by adjacent transpositions, swaps of neighboring items lifted into the permutation. The target is the canonical cyclic permutation, a standard reference form. They ask how many steps the hardest case can take.

They prove upper and lower bounds on that maximal step count. They also bound the diameter of the underlying Schreier graph. Diameter is the longest shortest path in that graph of states. Sorting time questions of this kind sit in combinatorics and computer science. Tight bounds tell us the true cost of sorting by such restricted moves.
arxiv-2601-13597:
Shyam Agarwal, Hao He, and Bogdan Vasilescu ask how AI coding tools change real software work in 2026. Some tools sit in the code editor and suggest lines as a person types. Newer agents act on their own, writing code and sending pull requests to merge it. The true effect of agents on live open-source projects is still not clear.

The team tracks agent use over time in many open-source code stores. They match projects that took up agents with like projects that did not. They then use a staggered diff-in-diff method to judge cause, not just links. The work aims to show what agents change, for good or ill.
arxiv-2601-13897:
Ankita Joshi and co-authors build an AI method to trace white matter fibers in the brain in 2026. Tractography rebuilds fiber pathways in a non-invasive way from scans. Those maps show brain connectivity and guide precise neurosurgery. Classic methods used deterministic and probabilistic rules to trace each fiber.

Deep learning and deep reinforcement learning have improved tract reconstruction in recent years. The team's TractRLFusion uses a GPT-based multi-critic policy fusion frame. Multiple critics judge each tracing policy, and their views are fused. Better tract maps could sharpen surgical plans and brain studies.
arxiv-2601-14197:
P. G. Beck and a large team weigh a star at a key life stage with two methods in 2026. Asteroseismology gives precise masses for solar-like oscillating stars. It uses individual frequency modeling or homological scaling relations. These methods have not been dynamically validated on the main sequence.

No eclipsing double-lined binary benchmark exists for that stage. The team measures a dynamical mass for a solar-like oscillator at the main sequence turnoff. They combine Gaia astrometry with ground-based spectroscopy. A dynamical mass can test if seismic masses are as true as claimed.
arxiv-2601-14297:
Tzula B. Propp, Brandy Todd, Sara A. Metwalli, and eight co-authors issue a call to action in this 2026 paper. Their field is quantum science. The year 2025 marked one hundred years since the discovery of quantum mechanics. In that century, the field grew into a global community. It now spans academics, engineers, developers, and entrepreneurs.

The authors write for that whole community. Their title says the paper is about meeting the needs of quantum scientists worldwide. It is a position piece, not a lab report. Readers get a view of what a broad team of insiders thinks the field must do next to serve its own people.
arxiv-2601-14497:
Noam Soker examines a fading star event in this 2026 paper. The event is M31-2014-DS1, a yellow supergiant in the Andromeda galaxy that dimmed sharply. One proposed account is a failed supernova. In that scenario, most of the yellow supergiant collapsed to form a black hole. Only a weak display reached the outside.

Soker tests that scenario and finds it wanting. He argues it requires unlikely fine-tuned parameters to work, if it works at all. His title calls it the failed failed-supernova scenario. Readers get a skeptical audit of a bold claim, with the fine-tuning cost laid out in the open.
arxiv-2601-14997:
K. Punnam Chandar and Y. Ravi Kumar describe how to turn CT scans into 3D printable models. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with medical images stored in DICOM format. Building a 3D STL model from 2D scan slices helps doctors grasp a structure's shape and any deformity.

The steps start with cleaning the CT images. Contrast is raised, noise is cut, and the images are smoothed. The cleaned scans are then split into regions by a threshold rule. From the 2D contours of those regions, the team rebuilds the full 3D model.
arxiv-2601-14697:
Shutong Qiao and five co-authors study generative recommendation in this 2026 paper, set for the ACM Web Conference. Semantic ID learning is a key interface in generative recommendation models. It maps items to discrete identifiers grounded in side information, most commonly via a pretrained text encoder. Those encoders are primarily optimized for well-formed natural language.

Real recommendation data are distinct. Item descriptions are often symbolic and attribute-centric, containing numerals, units, and abbreviations. The team runs an empirical study of what happens when text-as-vision meets semantic IDs in this setting. Lists there are terse and full of codes, not neat prose. A good ID is a small thing with a big job. It must hold all the facts a shop keeps on a thing. Readers get evidence on whether image-like renderings of item text serve recommenders better than raw text.
arxiv-2601-16097:
Makbule Ozsoy works on ways to turn words in many tongues into graph queries. Her 2026 preprint deals with tools that turn plain speech into code for data stores. Such tools exist for text to SQL and kin tasks. Most past work backs speech in just one tongue, English. True use needs the same skill in many tongues at once.

Ozsoy joins small add on parts, called adapters, into one fused tool. The join uses both fixed mix rules and learned mix gates. Fused parts let one tool serve many tongues with less cost. The work aims to open graph data stores to more users. It tests if fusion beats a lone part per tongue.
arxiv-2601-16297:
Ryuichiro Kitano and Shohei Okawa link the cut off of the Standard Model to proton death. Their 2026 preprint deals with why no proton death has yet been seen. It also deals with why neutrino mass is so small. Both facts may stem from chance guards in the known model. Those guards hold as long as no death terms sit at low scale.

The pair ask how high the model can run sans new terms. That top scale is the cut off of the model. A high cut off would leave death too slow to see yet. It would also keep neutrino mass small in a plain way. The work ties two null finds to one scale.
arxiv-2601-16397:
Qianqi Yan and coauthors cite proof as they write short forms of ward cases. Their 2026 preprint deals with sums that join text and pics in care. Trust needs more than smooth text from such tools. Each claim in a sum should point to its source span. Past tools oft add cites post hoc, with weak links to truth.

The new frame cites spans and pics as text is built. It uses the gaze weights of the coder to find source spans. No fresh train is needed for the cite step. Live cites let ward staff check claims with speed. The work seeks trust in AI ward sums.
arxiv-2601-16697:
Hitomi Mori, Yuta Kikuchi, Marcello Benedetti, and Matthias Rosenkranz probe the true cost of quantum tools. Some quantum tools solve sets of linked math tasks. Such tasks sit at the core of many quantum apps. Their cost is gauged by calls to a data source. Their 2026 preprint sets a floor on that cost.

The floor turns on how sparse the task's grid is. Sparse grids have few non-null marks in each row. The team proves no tool can beat their floor. Such floors tell builders what gains are even in reach. They also show where sparse tasks stay cheap or dear.
arxiv-2601-16797:
Paulo dos Santos, João Mendes, José de Almeida, and Luís Coelho speed a key task in nano-optics. Tiny metal bits can trap light at their skins. That trap hums at a set tone for each bit shape. Labs need that tone to build sensors and light tools. Full wave sims give true tones but run slow.

Their 2026 preprint takes a leaner path for odd shapes. The path treats each bit as a set of small poles. It skips the heavy grid work of full sims. Fast tones let teams scan many shapes in a day. That pace aids design of chips that sense germs or gas.
arxiv-2601-16897:
Antesh Upadhyay, Sang Bin Moon, and Abolfazl Hashemi join four fixes for learn-by-crowd AI. Crowd learn trains one model from many phones or sites. No raw data leaves each site in that scheme. Four plagues hit it: rules, slow links, local steps, and drop-outs. Their 2026 preprint, FedSGM, treats all four in one frame.

The frame swaps steps by a switch rule as it goes. It needs no costly dual weights or sub-solves. Tight links are squeezed both ways in the frame. Part crowds can join or leave with no break. Such frames suit health and phone AI at scale.
arxiv-2601-17497:
Mohammed Barhoush, Arthur Mehta, Anne Müller, and Louis Salvail ask if top-grade security can exist for quantum functional encryption. Functional encryption lets users compute set functions on locked data. The ideal shield is simulation security. In the classical world, that ideal is known to be impossible. Those proofs, though, rest on classical steps.

Quantum rules may open or close new paths. The authors test if the ban holds in the quantum case. Their answer shapes what quantum crypto can promise. Overpromised security is a real-world risk. A firm bound tells builders what to aim for. The work sits where quantum physics meets data privacy.
arxiv-2601-17697:
Zexi Jia, Jinchao Zhang, and Jie Zhou present StyleDecoupler for artistic style analysis. Style is deeply entangled with content in images. That mix makes style hard to represent alone. The authors use an information-theoretic frame. Their key insight compares model types. Multi-modal vision models encode both style and content. Uni-modal models suppress style and keep content traits.

That contrast gives a lever to split the two. A clean style code serves art search, forgery checks, and creative tools. Generalizable splitting must work on new artists and forms. The frame aims for that breadth. It turns a quirk of model training into a tool. Style science gains a principled path forward.
arxiv-2601-17597:
Shih-Yu Chang builds spectral tools for noncommuting operators. Classical spectral theory fully describes one normal operator. It fails when operators do not commute. No joint spectrum or shared diagonal form exists then. Past approaches each cover part of the gap. Joint spectra fit commuting families. Other methods stress global traits and hide local structure.

Chang offers categorified spectral sheaves and homotopical invariants. Sheaves track local data across a space in a glued way. That fits the local structure gap in past work. Noncommuting operators rule quantum systems with mixed controls. Better spectral tools aid both math and physics. The work seeks a language for spectra that never align.
arxiv-2601-18197:
Shaokang Wang and co-authors build a data flywheel that trains critic models for screen agents. Their 2026 preprint presents GAIA. Vision-language models have made GUI agents far better at reading screens and following instructions. One flaw stands out: agent actions cannot be undone. A single wrong click can cascade into a failed or harmful run. Critic models that judge actions before they run could catch such errors, and test-time scaling lets agents try more options.

GAIA gathers data in a loop that keeps improving those critics. Better critics make safer, more reliable agents. The flywheel idea ties data growth to model growth. The work targets a trust problem at the heart of computer-using AI.
arxiv-2601-18997:
Mélanie Gaillochet, Christian Desrosiers, and Hervé Lombaert make error bars for medical image models respect anatomy. Doctors need to know how much to trust a model's outline of an organ or a tumor. Conformal prediction gives error bounds with strict odds backing, but plain use can yield broken, patchy sets.

Those patchy sets ignore the body's layout and are hard to use in clinic. The team adds random walks that follow anatomy, so the sets stay in one piece and match real structures. Trustworthy bounds that look like anatomy could help doctors act on model output with more care.
arxiv-2601-19197:
Sushant Mehta builds a human centered way to grade chat based recommenders. Language models have given recommenders new skills: they understand plain requests, explain picks, and hold a conversation. Old grading methods, though, focus on classic scores like accuracy of the ranked list.

Those scores miss how the system treats the person using it. The framework, HELM, adds the human side to the grade: trust, clarity, and the feel of the exchange. As recommenders turn into chat partners, grading what users experience matters as much as grading the list itself.
arxiv-2601-19297:
Karl Schrader and three co-authors rebuild a sound field's strength from sparse measures, without its phase. In acoustics, phase is often unreliable or out of reach, yet knowing where sound is strong matters for rooms and devices. Their method uses physics informed neural networks, which bake the wave laws into the learning.

Phase retrieval, a classic trick for recovering lost phase, guides the network's training. Sparse sensors plus sound laws could map a whole room's sound from a few microphones. That serves concert hall design, noise control, and any task where placing many sensors is not an option.
arxiv-2601-19597:
Yichao Cai, Zhen Zhang, Yuhang Liu, and Javen Qinfeng Shi examine how contrastive learning shapes data. Contrastive methods train models to pull similar items together and push different ones apart. The InfoNCE objective powers most of these systems. Its geometry, though, is understood mainly through a simple split into alignment and uniformity.

The authors build a measure-theoretic framework for the process. Learning is modeled as the slow evolution of a cloud of representations on a fixed surface. They prove that in the large-batch limit, the random training objective matches a deterministic energy. That bridge lets them describe the forces shaping the cloud. A clearer picture of these dynamics could guide better self-supervised learning.
arxiv-2601-19897:
Idan Shenfeld, Mehul Damani, Jonas Hübotter, and Pulkit Agrawal show that models can keep learning by teaching themselves. Continual learning means gaining new skills without degrading old ones. It remains a fundamental challenge for foundation models. On-policy reinforcement learning can reduce forgetting, but it needs explicit reward functions, which are often unavailable.

The main alternative, learning from expert demonstrations, is dominated by supervised fine-tuning. That method is inherently off-policy, which works against it here. The authors show self-distillation enables continual learning instead. The model generates its own training signal from its current behaviour. If robust, the approach frees continual learning from both rewards and fresh demonstrations.
arxiv-2601-20197:
Raphaël Langevin studies bias in the estimation of finite mixture models, which are used in economics to capture hidden differences between people or firms. He shows that maximum likelihood estimation of such mixtures can suffer large finite-sample bias in all parameters, even under mild conditions. The paper is a revision of an earlier draft on consistent estimation of mixtures.

The application is to latent group structures in panel data, where units fall into unobserved groups. If the bias is ignored, researchers may report group effects that are mostly noise. A bias-reduced estimator would make studies of grouped panel data more trustworthy.
arxiv-2601-18397:
Debajyoti Dutta and three colleagues test neat patterns for how neutrinos mix as they fly. Neutrinos shift from one kind to the next as they move, and a small table of angles sums up that shift. Some grand plans for the laws of taste predict that one whole row or column of that table stays fixed.

A new test in China has now pinned one of those angles with great care. That pin cuts off part of the neat patterns at once. The rest make sharp links between a second angle and a phase that sets how matter and anti-matter part ways. Two big planned tests, one in the States and one in Japan, can check those links. A hit or a miss would tell us much about the deep rules that shape taste in the small world.
arxiv-2601-18497:
Sizhe Cheng and three colleagues use a trick of the eye to guard phone charts from prying looks. Phone charts can show health, cash, or work facts in a public place. A bystander who glances at the screen may read more than the owner would share. Past guards blur or dim the chart, but they spoil the view for the owner too.

Their tool, named BAIT, stacks a fake chart on top of the true one. The eye of a bystander, at a slant, picks up the fake chart. The owner, face on, still reads the true chart with ease. The stack is built by a tool that takes any chart as its start. A guard like this could make phone charts safe to use on trains and in queues.
arxiv-2601-18797:
Amin Hashemi and four colleagues build a chip that can set the traits of light that is part way between neat and wild. Neat light, like a laser's, has waves in step. Wild light has them at odds. Part-way light sits between, and it can do tricks in talk and in code work that neat light can't. Till now those tricks were shown with big bench kit that can't be chained at scale.

Their chip works on four streams of such light at once. It can set how the streams link, how wild they run, and how their traits chart as one. A chip form could let those tricks grow to large nets of light. The team chart the chip's reach trait by trait. Such chips may one day sit in fast talk links that use part-way light as a plus, not a flaw.
arxiv-2601-18897:
Qusai Khaled and three colleagues build a tool that not just guesses the power use of a waste water plant, but tells how sure the guess is, and why. Such plants burn a small but real share of the world's power. A good guess of their next use helps crews run them at less cost and with less waste. Past smart tools give one count with no tale of its doubt. In a plant where a wrong call can do harm, that is not enough.

Their tool is built from fuzzy rules that a human can read. It gives a range for the next use, not just a point. The width of the range tells the crew how far to trust the guess. A clear range could help crews plan pumps and stores with care. It brings doubt into the open where it can be used.
arxiv-2601-21197:
Dimitar Grantcharov, Khoa Nguyen, and Kaiming Zhao study a family of modules tied to a small but central algebra in math. The algebra, known as sl(2), shows up across geometry and physics. They look at its simple modules that stay free of rank two over a smaller, well-behaved part.

The authors describe this family in full. Knowing the simple building blocks helps classify wider classes of representations. Rank two is the first case where the structure gets rich enough to be hard. Their result gives later work a firm base for the next cases.
arxiv-2601-21597:
Marco Vallone studies light-matter states leaking out of hybrid plasmonic cavities. These tiny cavities are prized for nanotechnology, but they lose energy through radiation and absorption. How those losses work decides whether the devices behave as hoped.

Treating the cavity as an open system, the author derives an equation that keeps interference between decay paths. Simpler treatments drop that interference as a shortcut. The full version reduces to the standard one when the surroundings can tell the states apart. Keeping the interference terms matters where paths overlap, since they can shield dark states from leaking.
arxiv-2601-22397:
Jianchang Su and five co-authors use a language model as the brain of an autoscaler for ML pipelines. Such pipelines run in stages, and load shifts can move the choke point from stage to stage. Their 2026 preprint, SAIR, notes that mixed gear and tight links make scaling hard to tune by hand.

SAIR lets the model learn on the job, from reward-tagged past acts, with no retraining of its weights. It aims to cut cost while holding speed and quality. The work fits cloud teams that serve models all day. It tests a new role for language models in systems control.
arxiv-2601-22597:
Ryo Fujii, Makoto Morishita, Kazuki Yano, and Jun Suzuki built TimeMachine-bench, a test for AI that migrates old code to new settings. Migration is daily work for engineers, yet AI tests have largely skipped it. Their 2026 preprint grades agents on repo-level moves, not toy edits.

A good bench shows whether an agent can handle the slog of real upkeep: stale calls, moved files, and version clashes. Scores here can guide firms that weigh AI help for legacy code. The work fills a plain gap in evaluation. It treats maintenance as a first-class skill.
arxiv-2601-22097:
Hongtian Yu and co-authors teach a particle detector to see like a camera. In high-energy physics, estimating the position and momentum of anti-neutrons from their traces in an electromagnetic calorimeter is crucial and hard. Anti-neutrons leave no track until they annihilate, so their parameters must be inferred from the resulting shower.

The team's 2026 preprint proposes the Vision Calorimeter, a framework that moves visual object detectors, the networks that find objects in photographs, into calorimeter analysis. Treating shower patterns as images lets the detector borrow mature computer vision machinery. Better anti-neutron measurement sharpens experiments that probe matter and antimatter, where every reconstructed particle tightens the physics conclusions.
arxiv-2601-22197:
Jathurshan Pradeepkumar, Zheng Chen, and Jimeng Sun turn brain recordings directly into clinical notes. Writing reports that summarize abnormal patterns and diagnostic findings from long-term EEG recordings is slow, expert work. Their 2026 preprint curates a large clinical EEG dataset to attack the problem.

The dataset pairs nearly ten thousand reports with roughly eleven thousand hours of recordings from just over nine thousand patients. With that scale, models can learn to generate clinical notes from raw neural signals in real-world settings, not just in the lab. Automated drafting could cut neurologists' reporting burden, though the generated notes would still need expert review before guiding care.
arxiv-2601-20697:
Yifan Bai, Clarice Poon, and Jingwei Liang work on a hard problem in sparse data fitting. Their 2026 paper concerns dimension reduction for models with overlapping group sparsity. In such models, variables are sorted into groups that can share members. A good fit uses only a few groups. Cutting the problem down to size first makes it far cheaper to solve.

For groups that do not overlap, screening rules are well developed. They rest on a dual certificate from the first-order optimality condition. Overlap breaks that neat picture. The subgradient structure grows more complex, and the link between the sparse pattern and the dual variable turns indirect. The authors build reduction rules that cope with the overlap. Their work aids fast fitting of grouped models in statistics and signal work.
arxiv-2601-20797:
Guillermo GP-Lenza and three co-authors set out a method for planning robot missions with knowledge graphs. Their 2026 paper targets autonomous robots that run on ROS 2, a standard robot software framework. A knowledge graph stores facts and links about the mission. Used well, it can make a robot's mission planning smarter and more efficient.

The method runs through several steps. The team defines the start and target conditions first. They then structure tasks and subtasks and plan their sequence. Task data is written into the knowledge graph. At the end, the mission is designed in a high-level language. The paper gives robot builders a full recipe, from first facts to a mission a robot can run.
arxiv-2601-20897:
Cihan Sabuncu studies whole numbers that hide a digit and split into two prime squares. The 2026 paper works in base g, an arbitrary counting base. Some integers omit a fixed digit in that base expansion. The paper asks which of them equal a sum of two prime squares. It weights the count by the von Mangoldt function, a standard tool in prime number theory.

The first part applies the Hardy-Littlewood circle method. That method is a classic engine for counting number-theoretic patterns. It yields asymptotic formulas for the weighted count of such representations. The count grows as the length bound tends to infinity. Results of this kind test how primes and digit rules interact. The paper adds a precise case to the study of numbers with missing digits.
arxiv-2601-20997:
Jarrett Moon and five co-authors propose a home-grown supply route for a key medical isotope. Their 2026 paper concerns technetium-99m, used in more than sixteen million US diagnostic procedures each year. Patients receive it from generators stocked with molybdenum-99. That parent isotope is made at nuclear reactors. The supply chain has several points of vulnerability. Shortages and delays can harm patient care.

The authors champion novel high-current cyclotrons to break the dependence. Their machines use deuterium beams for compact neutron generation. Those neutrons would drive molybdenum-99 production on domestic soil. The title's path runs from beam to bedside. The paper makes the case for resilient, local supply. It joins physics, engineering, and health policy in one plan.
arxiv-2512-01197:
Yuzuru Inahama studies random paths that jiggle with long memory. In his setup, noise comes from fractional Brownian motion. That noise keeps a trace of its past, unlike plain random steps. The paths that result are called fractional diffusion paths.

Inahama asks what those paths look like when they must end at a set point. A path forced to hit a fixed end is called a bridge. He builds the math for these fractional bridges. Such bridges help in fields where a random path must be tied to a known start and end, like in finance or physics.
arxiv-2512-01297:
Shruti Rastogi and Vaibhav Vaish study the intersection complex of a threefold as a motive. The intersection complex is a tool that tracks the shape of singular spaces. Morel's work framed it through weight cuts. That frame drives the new work.

The pair build a new object in the world of motivic sheaves. It is made for set schemes and weight profiles. Their object aims to capture the intersection complex in motive terms. Work at this level helps unify how singular spaces are counted and compared across geometry fields. A motive-level form also lets the complex be moved and compared across base changes, which older forms did not allow with ease.
arxiv-2512-01797:
Cheng Gao and co-authors hunt for neurons tied to hallucinations in language models. Models often state false facts with full confidence. Past work blamed data or training goals at a broad level. Neuron-level causes stayed largely unexplored until now.

The team finds a set of neurons linked to hallucination acts. They study the impact and origin of those neurons. If a small set drives many false claims, targeted fixes become feasible. Neuron-level insight could lead to monitors that flag risky outputs as they form. Hallucination neurons may cluster by fact type, which would let monitors watch the riskiest sets during high-stakes use like medicine.
arxiv-2512-00697:
Amichai Lampert, Andrew Snowden, and Tamar Ziegler work on a classic problem in number theory in a 2025 paper. Birch's theorem, from 1957, says that a set of polynomial forms of odd degree always has a nontrivial zero, if there are enough variables. A zero is an input, other than all zeros, that makes every form vanish.

Birch's proof gave no clear bound on how many variables are enough. Lampert and his coauthors prove polynomial bounds for that threshold, over any number field. Explicit bounds turn a pure existence result into something other mathematicians can use and check.
arxiv-2512-00797:
Nan Sun and five coauthors propose a new shape for robot intelligence in a 2025 paper. Foundation models now unify perception and planning in robotics, promising one model that sees, thinks, and acts. Real service work, though, is spread out, fast changing, and shared among people and robots.

Vision-language models read scenes well but lack a body-aware sense of action and lean on hand-crafted skills. The authors turn a single monolithic model into an embodied multi-agent architecture. Several agents split the cognitive work and coordinate with people. A team design like this may fit messy real workflows better than one giant model.
arxiv-2512-00897:
Kfir Eliaz and Ran Spiegler model a data monopolist in a 2025 economics paper. Imagine one firm that curates a database for users who want to learn a changing parameter. Some users, nowcasters, want the parameter's current value. Others, forecasters, care about its long-run value.

Storing data costs the firm a constant amount per unit. The monopolist designs a menu of contracts, each pairing a fee with a level of data access. The paper studies what menu a profit-maximizing firm would offer, a practice the title calls monopolistic data dumping. The results speak to pricing and access in today's data markets.
arxiv-2512-00997:
Param Biyani and four coauthors introduce IndiMathBench in a 2025 paper on machine-checked math. Autoformalization turns worded math problems into formal statements a theorem prover can check. Even with strong language models, doing this reliably is hard, and good training data is a major bottleneck.

Expert annotation takes deep skill in both math and theorem proving. IndiMathBench is a human-verified benchmark for evaluating mathematical theorem proving. It was curated with an AI-powered, human-assisted pipeline that formalizes natural language problems in the Lean language. A trusted benchmark shows whether autoformalization tools are ready for real mathematical work.
arxiv-2512-01097:
Zachary Terner, Alexander Petersen, and Yuedong Wang present Smart Bayes in a 2025 statistics paper. Classification can be generative, modeling how each class produces data, or discriminative, learning the class boundary directly. Naive Bayes is the classic generative method, while logistic regression is the classic discriminative one.

Smart Bayes bridges the two. It feeds ratio-based features from the first approach into a logistic-style classifier. From the first side, it relaxes Naive Bayes's fixed unit weights, letting the data set the weights on ratio features instead. The hybrid could keep Naive Bayes's stability on small data while gaining the sharper boundaries of the second.
arxiv-2601-22797:
Francesco Foggetti and six co-authors study how to get stronger terahertz pulses from layered magnetic materials. A fast laser pulse hits a stack of magnetic and non-magnetic films. The hit drives a brief spin current, which turns into a pulse of terahertz light.

What is still unclear is how to tune the strength and the range of tones in that pulse. The authors test how the stack design shapes the output. Better sources of terahertz light could serve imaging, security scans, and fast wireless links. Spin-based sources like these are valued because they are compact, efficient, and tunable by design of the magnetic layers.
arxiv-2601-23197:
Pietro Benetti Genolini, Oliver Janssen, and Sameer Murthy examine which complex metrics are allowed in a gravitational path integral. The integral in question computes the supersymmetric index, a protected count in quantum gravity. A criterion by Kontsevich, Segal, and Witten decides when a complex metric is allowable.

The authors focus on saddle points that capture supersymmetric black holes in five-dimensional anti-de Sitter space. Checking allowability there tests whether those black hole contributions are legitimate. The work sharpens the math behind black hole entropy counts. Saddle points for supersymmetric black holes in anti-de Sitter space are the concrete case the allowability discussion examines.
arxiv-2512-00097:
Proving olympiad geometry theorems by computer has long been a test of machine reasoning. Boyan Duan and a team of co-authors present a method for International Mathematical Olympiad level problems in 2025. Their solver is described as reaching gold-medal level while running entirely on ordinary CPUs.

The method relies on efficient heuristic choices of auxiliary constructions, the extra lines and points that unlock a geometry proof. It avoids neural network inference altogether. A fast CPU-only prover could make theorem proving cheaper and easier to inspect. Each step follows explicit geometric reasoning rather than a learned model's guesses. Geometry proofs are a demanding test because one wrong construction ruins the whole argument.
arxiv-2512-00297:
Checking whether several automata can accept one common input sounds simple, but it can be surprisingly hard. Michael Wehar revisits lower bounds for this intersection non-emptiness problem in 2025, for deterministic finite automata. The aim is unconditional results about time and space complexity.

Earlier conditional bounds, from Kasai and Iwata in 1985, tied the problem's difficulty to algorithms for nondeterministic logarithmic space. Wehar first strengthens those conditional time bounds as a step in the argument. Lower bounds matter because they tell algorithm designers when to stop hunting for faster methods and design around the hardness instead. The problem is also called DFA intersection, a staple of automata theory courses.
arxiv-2512-00497:
The EPR paradox challenges whether quantum mechanics completely describes reality, through entangled particles measured far apart. Henryk Gzyl reexamines the paradox for systems with finitely many levels in 2025. The analysis emphasizes the connection between measurements and conditional probabilities.

When a measurement is performed, the quantum state and the probability distribution become functions of the observable being measured. That observation reframes parts of the paradox in the language of chance. Finite-level systems are the ones actually built in laboratories, so sorting out the paradox there keeps the base of quantum theory tied to practice. Finite-level systems include the qubits and qudits of real quantum devices. Conditional chance is the language in which test outcomes are in fact reported. For a reader new to the field, the gain is a fresh eye. Old rifts are recast in terms of what a test can show, and what it can not show.
arxiv-2512-00597:
Medical vision-language models promise one system for many clinical imaging tasks, but volumetric CT remains hard. Thuraya Alzubaidi, Farhad Nezami, and Muzammil Behzad introduce MedCT-VLM in 2025, a parameter-efficient framework for adapting large CT foundation models. They use cross-modal low-rank adaptation.

Foundation models show strong zero-shot ability across image domains, yet their use in volumetric medical imaging is limited. Low-rank adaptation updates only a small set of added parameters, keeping adaptation cheap enough for hospitals. Efficient clinical models could bring foundation-model assistance to radiology departments without supercomputing budgets. Volumetric scans are three-dimensional, so adapting flat-image models is not straightforward. Low-rank updates are small enough to share between hospitals for comparison. For scan teams in small towns, the gain is reach. A big model can be trimmed to fit their kit, and still read chest scans with care and speed.
arxiv-2512-03397:
Robots and drones need to know where they are without GPS. Seungwon Choi, Dong-Gyu Park, Seo-Yeon Hwang, and Tae-Wan Kim present Surfel-LIO in this 2025 work. It is a LiDAR-inertial odometry system, blending laser scans with motion sensors.

Recent advances in map structures have made such systems faster. Surfel-LIO pre-computes surfels, small surface patches, and uses a hierarchical voxel hashing scheme. Fast, accurate tracking matters in tunnels, warehouses, and disaster sites. The design aims for real-time speed without losing precision. Pre-computed surfels shift work ahead of time, which frees the live system for speed.
arxiv-2512-02097:
When particles collide slowly, the rules of quantum mechanics demand that probability is never created or destroyed, a constraint called unitarity. Marcos Flores and Kalliopi Petraki build in 2025 a tidy scheme for non-relativistic scattering that respects that demand while joining elastic and inelastic channels.

Inelastic channels, where collisions change the particles' internal state, secretly shape the elastic ones through the optical theorem. The authors show those effects can be deduced consistently, leading to non-local separable potentials and a compact unitarization scheme. Getting unitarity right matters for effective theories of dark matter and nuclei, where scattering calculations must not leak probability.
arxiv-2512-02297:
Fifth-generation mobile networks are becoming software systems, with the radio access network steered by small applications called xApps. Philip Rodgers and Paul Harvey propose in 2025 an xApp Store, a framework for bringing such apps on board and deploying them in open RAN networks.

The app-store model invites third-party developers into an ecosystem that was once closed to a few vendors, much as phone apps once did. Onboarding needs vetting, packaging, and deployment machinery that telecom lacks today. A working store framework could diversify who builds the intelligence inside future mobile networks.
arxiv-2512-02397:
Clusters in data can be judged by how their points spread in space and by how the mass is shared among them, and the two views need not agree. Emanuele Bossi, C. Tyler Diggans, and Abd AlRahman AlMomani introduce in 2025 the Boltzmann-Shannon Index, a normalized measure of density balance across clusters.

The index compares a geometry-based distribution over clusters with a frequency-based one, quantifying how similar the clusters' densities are. A single balance score helps analysts compare clusterings and spot lopsided groupings. Clustering underlies customer segmentation, image grouping, and exploratory science, so better quality measures propagate widely.
arxiv-2512-02797:
Sebastian Zieglmeier and four co-authors schedule data driven control across the working range of a nonlinear system. Data enabled predictive control steers a system using recorded behavior instead of a physics model. One global dataset struggles when the system behaves differently in different regimes.

Their gain scheduled version splits the range of a measurable scheduling variable into regions. Each region gets its own Hankel matrix, built from rich recorded data. Control then blends these local descriptions as conditions change. The approach suits engines, robots, and processes whose dynamics shift with speed or load. Local charts for each zone keep the math lean, since each chart need span just its own small patch of work.
plos-pone-0010197:
The authors were Sujatha Srinivasan, Congzhou Liu, Caroline Mitchell, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study sampled vaginal bacteria in women over short periods. Little was known about how quickly those bacterial communities change day to day. The team used PCR tests to track key bacteria in healthy women, and in women treated with antibiotics for bacterial vaginosis.

Bacterial vaginosis is an imbalance of the normal vaginal community, not a single germ. Tracking short-term swings shows how stable healthy communities are and how fast treatment shifts them. That timing knowledge can improve diagnosis and follow-up care for a very common condition.
plos-pone-0009897:
Proteins often work in teams, joining into complexes with shared surfaces. Giovanni Feverati and Claire Lesieur put those joining surfaces under a new lens. Their tool, called Gemini, appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Oligomers are small clusters of protein subunits.

An oligomeric interface is where protein subunits touch and bind. Studying those contacts explains how complexes hold together and fall apart. Gemini examines interfaces in a systematic way across many proteins. The view helps researchers predict assembly and design drugs that block it. Subunits that fit poorly cannot build a working complex.
plos-pone-0009997:
Fat cells grow larger in obesity, but not all fat depots carry the same health risk. Jean O'Connell and colleagues compared fat cell sizes in people with severe obesity. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

The two depots are omental fat, deep in the belly, and subcutaneous fat, under the skin. Adipocyte size from each depot was set against metabolic disease markers. Severe obesity means a body mass far above the healthy range. Belly fat is long suspected of driving diabetes and heart risk. The comparison tests whether cell size itself tracks that danger.
